title: Opus 5.5, in plain words.
subtitle: What changed, which Claude and effort to pick, and a six-step way to make it check its own work:

title: Claude, past the basics.
subtitle: Twenty-six small habits that save time, usage and mistakes:
text: Getting one good answer out of Claude is the easy part. The rest of the week is where things slip. The chat that runs so long it eats into your limits. The number that went into a report without a check. The background you explain again, and again. The limit that arrives halfway through a task. A better prompt won't fix those. Small habits will. I teach people to use AI at work. These are the habits I'd want every one of them to have. Each one rests on a documented Claude feature or on Anthropic's own advice, linked where it's Anthropic's. Most take one click or one sentence. Here are twenty-six, in six groups: Set it up once (habits 1 to 3) Ask so the first answer lands (4 to 9) Projects, files and artifacts (10 to 14) Check before you trust (15 to 18) Make your usage last (19 to 22) Hand bigger jobs to Cowork (23 to 26) Each habit has the clicks, the reason, a prompt to copy and a graphic. New to Claude? Start with Claude, from the first click, then come back. Set it up once Three settings that shape every chat after them. 1. Write your Instructions once Caught yourself typing "shorter" or "no jargon" again? A correction you make twice belongs in Instructions. Where: click your initials in the lower left corner, then Settings → Your Claude → Instructions. In the older Settings layout, that page is called Account. Why it works: anything you add there applies to all of your conversations. You stop paying for the same correction in every chat. Anthropic suggests four things to put there: the approaches or methods you prefer the terms you use the situations you often face how you want Claude to communicate In the new Claude experience, Cowork's Global instructions moved into this box too. When to use it: once, then whenever you catch yourself repeating a correction. I work as [your role] in [your field]. Write in plain English: short paragraphs, no jargon, no filler. Start long answers with a three-line summary. When I say "[a term you use]", I mean [what it means]. If something important is missing, ask me before you start. Not sure what to write? Let Claude draft it from a chat where it got you right. When to use it: at the end of a chat that went well. Based on this chat, draft Instructions for Claude that I can paste into Settings. Keep them under 120 words, in four short parts: how I like to work, the terms I use, the situations I often face, and how you should talk to me. Leave out anything that only applies to this one task. Read what comes back, cut anything too specific, then paste it in. Keep it general. One project's details go in its project instructions (habit 10). 2. Read what Claude remembers, and fix it Claude keeps a memory of you. On the Free, Pro, Max and Ultra plans, it's on by default. On Team and Enterprise, your organisation's owners decide. It saves what it learns as topics while you chat. Mention that a deadline moved, and your next conversation already knows. Useful, until something it remembers goes out of date. Where: Click your initials, then Settings → Your Claude. Click Manage next to Your memory. Everything is listed under Topics. Open one, then use the edit icon to fix it, or Delete to remove it. Why it works: fix a topic once, and every conversation from then on uses the fixed version. Each project keeps its own memory too. Moving from another AI assistant? On the same page, Start import shows a prompt to run in your old service. Paste what it gives you, then click Add to memory. Anthropic calls import experimental. Only memory comes across, not your old chats. When to use it: when something about you changes, or Claude gets a detail about you wrong twice. Please update your memory: I no longer [the old detail]. I now [the new detail]. Forget anything that says otherwise. The change applies from your next conversation. 3. Switch memory off before a one-off chat Helping a friend with their CV, or asking about something that shouldn't shape later answers? Turn memory off for that one chat. Do it before your first message: you can't change it later. Start a new chat. Click + in the message box. Click Memory to turn it off, then send your message. A crossed-out memory icon then appears next to the chat title. Claude won't use its memory there, and saves nothing from it. Want it out of your chat history too? Use an incognito chat: the ghost icon, upper right, in a new chat outside a project. Memory off for one chat Incognito chat Uses or adds to your memory No No Stays in your chat history Yes No Found when Claude searches past chats Yes No Can make files and run code As in any chat Not in the new Claude experience How to start it + → Memory, before you send Ghost icon, upper right Incognito chats aren't used for training. They're kept for 30 days by default. When to use it: when you shared something in a normal chat that Claude shouldn't keep. Please forget what I told you about [the topic]. Don't use it in future conversations. Set up Claude properly: the toolkit issue Ask so the first answer lands Six habits for the minute before you press send, each from Anthropic's own guidance. 4. Plan the chat, then send one full message Anthropic's first tip for getting more from your plan: plan the conversation before you begin. Know what you need. Group related questions into one message. Give the background up front. Paste the whole text you want edited, not one piece at a time. Then read your message once, and fix it before you send. Why it works: a clear first message saves a round of follow-ups. And Anthropic lists the length of the current chat among the things that use your limits faster. When to use it: any time you have more than one question about the same piece of work. I'm preparing [the piece of work] for [who it's for]. Here's what I have: [paste it, or attach the file]. Please answer these together: 1. [first question] 2. [second question] 3. [third question] Put each answer under its own heading. If you need anything else from me, ask before you start.…

title: Right tool, right job.
subtitle: Stop looking for one AI that does everything. Five everyday jobs, and where to start for each:
text: You use one AI for everything. Emails. Reports. Spreadsheets. Research. Slides. Some days it's brilliant. Some days it's clumsy, and you can't tell why. Often the problem is the match between the tool and the job. Each tool is built around different strengths. The companies say so themselves, in their own help pages. So stop hunting for the one AI that wins at everything. Pick the right one for each job instead. I teach people to use AI at work, and this is the question I hear most: "Which AI should I use?" My honest answer: it depends on the job. Here's where to start for five of them. Inside: One rule before any tool Deep work and writing Spreadsheets Search and research Work in other languages Presentations The whole map on one page How to test a tool on your own work A quick promise: I didn't run a test or a ranking for this issue. Every choice below comes from what each company documents about its own product. Treat each one as where to start, then judge on your own work. One rule before any tool Here it is: Start with the tool built around the job, then keep it only if it works on your own material. That's it. Three things follow from it. Where your work lives matters. If your numbers live in Excel, an AI that works inside Excel beats copying and pasting. The documented feature matters more than the hype. A tool that says it gives sources, keeps formulas or uses your template is telling you what it was built for. Your own test beats anyone's ranking. Including mine. You don't need five subscriptions for this. Several tools below have free plans, and the free version of this map shows where each free plan stops. Whatever tool you pick, it can be wrong. Anthropic says plainly not to rely on Claude as a single source of truth, and to check cited sources on anything high-stakes. The same habit applies to every AI here. Deep work and writing Try first: Claude, on Opus 5.5. This is the long, careful work. A report. A proposal. A difficult email. Making sense of a pile of documents. Why Claude for this: Anthropic's own advice is to start with Opus 5.5 if you're unsure, and it calls it the "strongest daily driver" for knowledge work. It's built for clear writing. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 puts the most important information up front, uses less jargon, and follows the writing rules you give it. It takes in a lot at once. On paid plans, Opus 5.5 has a 1M-token context window in chat. ChatGPT's published windows run from 27K to 400K, depending on plan and model. Projects keep your material in one place, with their own chats and files. Free users can create up to five. One thing to know: on the Free plan, Claude offers Sonnet and Haiku, not Opus. Opus 5.5 starts on Pro. To pick it, click the model name next to the send button and choose Opus 5.5, or click More models. I've attached my notes, the client's brief and last quarter's report. Write a first draft of a two-page proposal for [client]. Audience: their operations director, who is busy and sceptical. Put the recommendation and the cost in the first paragraph. Plain English, short paragraphs, no jargon. Before you write, list anything in my notes that contradicts the brief, and ask me about it. The last line matters. It makes Claude check before it writes, instead of guessing. For quick, well-scoped jobs, Anthropic positions Sonnet 5.5 as strongest at everyday tasks and polished documents. Move down to it when Opus feels slow. guide:brief-claude-like-a-colleague Spreadsheets Try first: whichever AI works inside the spreadsheet you already use. This is the job where "where your work lives" matters most. If you live in Excel: Claude for Excel Claude for Excel is an add-in that works inside your workbook. Anthropic's docs say it: answers questions about your workbook with cell-level citations, so you can see where a number came from adjusts assumptions while keeping formulas intact debugs errors and builds models It runs on Excel on the web, Windows and Mac. Its docs list Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans. To install it, find the Claude for Microsoft 365 listing on Microsoft AppSource, click Get it now, then sign in with your Claude account. Look at the Forecast sheet. Explain in five plain sentences how next year's revenue figure is built, citing the cells you used. Then change the growth assumption from 8% to 5% and tell me which totals move. Don't overwrite any formula. If you want charts from a file: ChatGPT data analysis ChatGPT's data analysis takes spreadsheets (.xls, .xlsx, .csv) and PDFs, and for some tasks writes and runs Python. It makes interactive bar, line, pie and scatter charts on Plus and Pro. To see the numbers behind a chart, open Chart options (•••) and choose View as table. On Free, data analysis is limited. If your team runs on Google Sheets: Gemini Gemini with Google Workspace puts AI inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets and Slides. For businesses it starts at $14 a seat per month. Whatever you use, ask for the working, not only the answer. A number with a cell reference or a table behind it is a number you can check. guide:ask-claude-about-your-data Search and research Try first: Perplexity for quick answers with sources. Claude Research or Gemini Deep Research for a full report. Search has two jobs hiding inside it. Quick, looked-up answers Perplexity is built around search. On its Free plan you get practically unlimited basic searches and 3 Pro Searches a day. Pro adds advanced models and 10x as many citations per answer. Claude can search too. Click + in the message box, then Web search, and the answers come back with citations. Free accounts can use it. A proper report When you need many searches that build on each other, use a research mode. Claude Research (paid plans) runs multiple searches across the web and your connected tools. Turn it on with + → Research. Gemini Deep Research is on Google's Free plan. Google says it can analyse hundreds of sources to write a research report. Anthropic's own rule of thumb is useful…

title: Proof gets you hired.
subtitle: Your AI certificates are a good start. Here's how to build the proof that comes next:
text: You finished the course. You passed the quiz. You added the certificate to your profile. Then nothing happened. No calls. No clients. No change at work. I want to be clear before anything else: that certificate was worth earning. I hold several myself. But a certificate is where proof starts. It isn't the proof. This issue is about the gap between the two, and how to close it. Inside: What a certificate really shows Why it can't stand on its own any more What an employer or client can actually check How to build one piece of proof, with AI as your coach How to write it up and put it where people look The one line never to cross Certificates are a good start I'm a data and AI leader and educator. My mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. I hold the Microsoft Professional Degree in Data Science. I'm a Celonis Analyst and Data Engineer. IBM gave me its Big Data Engineer Mastery Award. I'm proud of every one of them. Each one made me learn things I'd have skipped on my own. Each one gave me a structure, a deadline and a test. That's what a good course does. Some good AI courses are free, too. Anthropic's learning site, Claude Academy, costs nothing. A free Claude account saves your progress and earns completion badges. Its "AI Fluency: Framework and foundations" course is 14 lessons, one quiz and about four hours. Google AI Essentials takes under five hours and needs no experience. In the U.S. and Canada it costs $49 a month after a seven-day free trial. So take the course. Learn the thing. Keep the certificate. A certificate tells people you learned something. Proof tells them what you can do with it. You want both. What a certificate actually shows Read the small print on any certificate and it's honest about what it is. Claude Academy says its badges record that you completed the course as it existed when you took it. The issue date sits on the verification page. You earn the badge by passing the quizzes. Every lesson quiz, plus any final assessment. Anyone can check it's genuine through a public link. That's real. It's also narrow. Here's what that same certificate can't show: the problem you'd solve on day one how you'd handle messy, real data or a vague brief whether you check AI's work before you send it how you explain a result to someone who isn't technical your judgment Claude Academy is careful here too. It says its completion badges are not certifications. Claude certification exams are a separate paid, proctored program, and only companies in Anthropic's partner program can get them. Different credentials test different things. That's fine, as long as you know which one you hold. Everyone has the certificate now Here's the uncomfortable part. Employers do want AI skills. The evidence is clear. In Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index, 66% of leaders said they wouldn't hire someone without AI skills. 71% said they'd rather hire a less experienced candidate with AI skills than a more experienced one without them. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 puts AI and big data at the top of the fastest-growing skills. Two-thirds of employers plan to hire people with specific AI skills. So people responded. The same Work Trend Index reported a 142x increase in LinkedIn members adding AI skills like ChatGPT and Copilot to their profiles. Think about what that means for you. If everyone lists the skill, the list stops telling anyone apart. LinkedIn's Skills on the Rise 2026 says employers increasingly prioritise skills over degrees, job titles or linear career paths. Skills. Not the line on the profile. And the most sought-after core skill in the WEF report isn't a tool at all. It's analytical thinking, essential for seven out of 10 companies. You can't show analytical thinking with a badge. You show it with work. What people can actually check Put yourself in the hiring manager's seat. Or the client's. They have a few minutes. What can they actually look at? What you show What they can check What it tells them A certificate or badge That it's genuine, and the date You finished a course and passed its quizzes A line on your profile ("AI skills") Nothing That you typed it A project they can open The thing itself: the sheet, the report, the tool What you can build A short write-up Your reasoning, step by step How you think, and how you checked A few pieces in one place A pattern over time That you keep doing it The bottom three rows are the ones that start conversations. They also give the interviewer something to ask about. "Walk me through this" is the easiest question in the world to answer when you did the work. Microsoft built some of its own credentials this way. Microsoft Applied Skills are earned by completing interactive tasks that align to real work, in a lab-based assessment. Microsoft says they show employers you can hit the ground running. Even the people who issue credentials want them to look more like real work. You can go one step further and show the real work itself. Build proof, with AI as your coach Proof doesn't need to be big. One small project, from a real problem, done well and explained clearly, beats ten certificates with nothing behind them. Here's how to build one. AI helps at every step, but as a coach. You do the work. It asks the questions, spots the gaps and pushes you. 1. Pick a real problem Start from your own work, or a cause or small business you care about. I want to build one small project that proves I can use AI well at work. About me: - My job or the job I want: [role] - Tools I use now: [e.g. Excel, Google Sheets, Claude, ChatGPT] - A task at work that is slow, repetitive or messy: [describe it] Suggest three project ideas I could finish in two weekends. For each one: the problem it solves, what I would build, what "done" looks like, and what a hiring manager would learn about me from it. Don't do the project. Ask me questions until we pick one. 2. title: Write it plain.
subtitle: AI drafts that sound like everyone else's? Here's the fix, step by step:
text: You ask Claude to write an email. It comes back fast, tidy and correct. And you can tell from the first line that a machine wrote it. Long words. Warm-up sentences. A summary at the end that repeats the start. Nothing is wrong with it. It just sounds like nobody. There's no magic phrase. What works is a small kit you set up once. I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. Plain writing is the skill that makes every AI draft more useful. What's inside: Why AI drafts come out bland What "plain" actually means, from official sources A short style instruction to add to every writing request A swap list of words and patterns to cut A research-first prompt to run before any piece of writing Ready-made versions for four everyday jobs A check you can run on any draft Why AI drafts come out bland Anthropic's prompting guide gives a useful picture. Treat Claude like a brilliant but new employee. Clever, but with no context on your norms or how your team works. Ask that new hire to "write an email to the client" and you'll get the safe, average email. The same guide says the more precisely you explain what you want, the better the result. So when you don't describe a style, Claude picks a default one. And the default is polished, formal and wordy. Three gaps cause most of it: No reader. Claude doesn't know who will read the piece, so it writes for everyone. No style. "Make it professional" is a mood, not an instruction. No facts. When the facts are thin, the words get fat. Filler fills the space. This issue closes all three gaps. Plain writing is about the reader, not about hiding that you used AI. The goal is a draft people understand on the first read. Brief Claude like a colleague What "plain" actually means "Write in plain English" sounds vague. It isn't. Governments have written it down in detail, because their readers include everyone. In the US, the Plain Writing Act of 2010 defines plain writing as writing that is clear, concise, well-organized and suited to the subject and audience. In the UK, plain English is mandatory for all of GOV.UK. The Government Digital Service points to literacy data: 1 in 6 adults in England has very poor literacy skills. And plain doesn't mean simple-minded. Digital.gov, which now carries selected PlainLanguage.gov guidance, puts "write for your audience" first. It calls "dumbing down" a common myth. You match your readers' knowledge, expertise and interest. So an expert reader can still get technical terms. A new customer gets everyday words. The rules, side by side Here's what three official sources say, in numbers you can hand to Claude. Rule GOV.UK Digital.gov Simplified Technical English Sentence length Try to split sentences over 25 words One idea per sentence 20 words for instructions, 25 for descriptions Paragraphs No more than 5 sentences 3 to 8 sentences, under 150 words, never over 250 One topic per sentence Voice Active: "You need an electronic travel authorisation" Everyday language Active, with commands for steps: "Install the component." Words Short over formal: "buy" not "purchase" Cut filler like "very" and "really" About 900 approved words, one meaning each Order Most important information first Write for your audience first Not stated The third column needs a word of explanation. Simplified Technical English (STE) is a controlled language first released in 1986 to help readers of English maintenance documentation. Its makers say it isn't meant for general writing. But they also say its principles, short sentences, one topic per sentence and the active voice, work well in other writing. That makes it a good model for one job in particular: instructions people must follow. Get the next issue by email The style instruction Here's the core of the kit. One short instruction that you add to every writing request. Or better, save once (next section). Two pieces of Anthropic's advice shape it. First, give the reason behind a rule. Anthropic's guide shows a bare rule, "NEVER use ellipses", next to a better one that explains the reply will be read aloud. With the reason, Claude can apply the idea to cases the rule never named. Second, say what to do, not only what to avoid. Ask for "flowing prose paragraphs" instead of "don't use markdown". So every line below says what to do, and most say why. Write in plain English for [who reads this: e.g. busy managers who read on their phones]. - Use short, everyday words: "buy" not "purchase", "help" not "assist", "use" not "utilise". Short words are faster to read. - Keep sentences under 25 words, with one idea each. Long sentences lose readers. - Put the most important point first. Most people scan and stop early. - Use the active voice and talk to the reader as "you". - Write short paragraphs of one to three sentences. Use a list only when order matters. - Explain any technical term in plain words the first time you use it. - Start with the answer and stop when you're done: no warm-up line, no closing summary. - Keep every fact I give you. Add no facts, numbers or quotes of your own. If something is missing, tell me. It's eight lines. That's deliberate. Anthropic's article for Claude app users warns that longer, more complex prompts are not always better. A few clear rules beat a pasted style manual. Fill in the first line for each job. The reader changes; the rules mostly don't. Add one example Words describe a style. An example shows it. Anthropic calls examples one of the most reliable ways to steer tone and structure. Its article for app users says to start with one and add more only if the output still doesn't match. It also warns that newer models pay very close attention to details in examples. So pick a clean one you'd be happy to see copied. Here is a short piece I wrote that sounds like me. Match its tone, sentence length and word choice. Don't copy its content. title: One good prompt.
subtitle: Getting bland, generic answers? Five rules and one template that fix them:
text: You ask Claude for something. It answers in seconds. Neat, polite, well organised. And completely generic. It could have been written for anyone. Most of the time, the cause is the prompt. And the prompt is the part you control. The good news: the fix is small, and Anthropic has written it down. I teach people to use AI at work, and this is the lesson that pays off fastest. So I've boiled Anthropic's own prompting guidance down to what you need in a normal working day. What's inside: Why answers come back generic Five rules that matter One template you can reuse for almost anything Ready-made versions for four everyday jobs The mistakes to stop making Where to save your rules so you never type them again Why answers come back generic Picture a brilliant new hire on their first morning. Sharp. Fast. Keen to help. But they don't know your team, your customers, your standards or why the task matters. Hand them a one-line request and they'll do the safest, most average version of it. That's exactly how Anthropic tells you to think about Claude. Its prompting guide says to treat Claude like a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows. And it adds: the more precisely you explain what you want, the better the result. So a generic answer is a signal. Claude filled the gaps with average guesses, because you left gaps. Anthropic also gives a simple test you can run on any prompt: Show your prompt to a colleague who knows little about the task. If they'd be confused about what to do, Claude will be too. Here's the same request at three levels of detail: Brief Claude like a colleague: the full guide Five rules that matter There are many prompting tricks. Most people need five. Each one comes from Anthropic's own guidance. 1. Give the goal and the context Say what you want, who it's for, and why. The "why" matters more than it looks. Anthropic's guide shows this with a rule: "NEVER use ellipses." On its own, it's a bare command. Add the reason (the reply will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine) and Claude can apply the idea to cases the rule never mentioned. So instead of a bare rule, give the reason behind it. Weak: "Keep it short." Strong: "Keep it under 100 words. My manager reads these on her phone between meetings." 2. Say what good looks like Claude can't read your mind about format. Anthropic's guide says to be specific about the output format and any limits. If order or completeness matters, ask for numbered or bulleted steps. And if you want more than the minimum, say so out loud. Claude won't assume you want the extra effort. One more detail from the same guide: tell Claude what to do, not what to avoid. Weak: "Don't use bullet points." Strong: "Write it as three short paragraphs of flowing prose." It also helps to write your prompt in the style you want back. A prompt full of bullets tends to get bullets. 3. Show one example Anthropic calls examples one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure. Its developer guide recommends three to five varied examples. Its article for people using the Claude apps is gentler: start with one, and add more only if the output still doesn't match. That article also warns that newer models pay very close attention to the details in examples. So pick your example with care. If it has a typo or a strange heading, you may get those back too. 4. Let Claude say "I don't know" Claude writes confidently even when it's wrong. Anthropic's help centre says plainly that Claude can "hallucinate" incorrect or misleading information. It says not to rely on Claude as your only source of truth, and to check cited sources and high-stakes advice. The simplest guard is one sentence. Anthropic's guide to reducing hallucinations says that explicitly giving Claude permission to say "I don't know" can drastically reduce false information. For long documents, the same guide adds two more moves: ask Claude to pull out word-for-word quotes first, then answer from those quotes ask it to back each claim with a quote, or take the claim back Anthropic is careful to say these reduce mistakes, but don't remove them. You still check. 5. Keep it short, and keep the rules few More words don't mean a better prompt. Anthropic's article for Claude app users warns against over-engineering: longer, more complex prompts are not always better. The same article says the first prompt rarely works perfectly. You test, then refine. It also says the heavy machinery is mostly optional now. XML tags and elaborate role-play are less necessary with modern models. Clear headings, white space and plain, explicit language work just as well for most jobs. A short role still helps. Anthropic says even a single sentence makes a difference to Claude's tone and behaviour. Something like "You're an experienced HR adviser" is enough. Three good rules beat fifteen vague ones. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 follows the writing rules you give it. That's a reason to give a few clear ones, and to make each one count. Before and after, side by side Here are the five rules as quick swaps. Instead of Try "Write a project update." "Write a project update for the finance director. She needs to decide on extra budget by Friday." "Make it professional." "Three short paragraphs, warm but direct, no jargon." "Don't make it too long." "Under 150 words: it's read on a phone." "Write it in our style." "Match the tone of this example: [paste one]." "What are the facts?" "If you're not sure of something, say so. Don't fill gaps with guesses." Fifteen rules in a row Three rules, each with a reason Notice what the right-hand column has in common. Every line answers a question a new colleague would ask you. The one-good-prompt template This is the template to keep. It puts the five rules in order, with brackets to fill in. Delete any line you don't need. You're [a role, in one sentence: e.g. an experienced editor for busy managers]. Goal: I need [the thing you want] so that [what it's for…

title: Bring the point.
subtitle: Using AI to write your LinkedIn posts? What it can't do for you, and what it can:
text: You asked AI for a LinkedIn post. It gave you one in ten seconds. Neat opening. Three tidy points. A question at the end. You posted it. A few likes. Then nothing. So you tried again. Same result. Here's the honest reason: the post had no point that was yours. AI can write. It can't decide what you know, what you believe, or who you're talking to. That part is your job. And it's the part that makes people stop scrolling. I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. This issue is the plain version of how to use AI on LinkedIn without sounding like everyone else. Inside: What LinkedIn itself says about AI-written posts Give before you take Break your own patterns Fix your visuals Steady beats a burst Decide who you want reading Prompts that keep your voice What LinkedIn says about AI posts Start with the rules of the room. LinkedIn has a help page called Best practices for content created with the help of AI. It says LinkedIn does not want "AI slop". Its definition: low-effort, likely AI-generated content that sounds polished but lacks a clear point of view, unique perspective or substance. Read that again. Sounds polished. That's exactly what a quick AI draft does well. The same page says LinkedIn judges whether content adds value, not how it was made. AI-assisted posts are welcome when they reflect a real person's perspective. Generic or repetitive posts are less likely to be widely distributed. And readers can now flag a post through its More menu with "Seems like AI slop". If a post gets enough of that feedback, its author sees a tip in Post analytics. LinkedIn says that's a tip, not a takedown. LinkedIn also asks you to review, edit and approve anything AI helped with. You're responsible for everything you post. If you relied heavily on AI and it isn't obvious, it suggests saying so. What a quick AI draft gives you What LinkedIn says it wants Polished sentences A clear point of view Safe, general advice A unique perspective The same shape as every other post Substance, from a real person Words nobody checked Content you reviewed, edited and approved AI is allowed. Empty is the problem. Bring the point, and let AI help you say it well. Nobody is waiting for your post This one stings a little. Nobody opens LinkedIn hoping to hear from you. They open it for themselves: to learn something, solve something, or feel less alone with a problem at work. LinkedIn's own words back this up. In its page on how the feed decides what to show, one of the content signals it lists is whether a post provides knowledge or advice. Others include what the post is about, how recent it is, and how constructive the conversation under it is. So the question for every post is simple. What does the reader walk away with? A method they can use tomorrow. A mistake they can now avoid. A number explained. A clear opinion they can argue with. If the honest answer is "they learn that I'm busy", rewrite it. Here's a prompt that makes AI ask you that question before it writes anything. I want to write a LinkedIn post about this: [paste your rough idea, a few lines is fine] Don't write the post yet. First, ask me five short questions, one at a time, to find out: 1. who exactly this is for 2. what they should be able to do or understand after reading 3. the one example or moment from my own work that proves it 4. what most people get wrong about this 5. what I actually believe that others might disagree with When I've answered all five, tell me in one sentence what the reader gets from this post. If you can't, tell me the idea isn't ready. The last line matters. A good assistant should be able to tell you "not yet". Know someone whose posts read like a press release? Send them this issue. Spot your own habits Look at your last ten posts. Same opening line style? Same length? Same three-point list? Same topic, every week? Your readers notice before you do. LinkedIn noticed too. When it announced changes to the feed in March 2026, it said it is showing less engagement bait and recycled content. The examples it gave: "comment to agree" prompts, and videos that don't match the text. And remember the AI page: generic or repetitive content is less likely to be widely distributed. AI makes repetition worse, because it reaches for the same shapes every time. Ask it for "a LinkedIn post" and you get the average LinkedIn post. So use AI the other way round: to spot your habits, not to repeat them. Below are my last ten LinkedIn posts, separated by ---. [paste them] Act as a blunt editor. Tell me: 1. the openings I keep reusing 2. the structures I keep reusing (lists, questions at the end, and so on) 3. the topics I keep circling back to 4. phrases that sound like any other post on LinkedIn 5. the one post that sounds most like me, and why Then suggest three different ways I could shape my next post. Don't write it. Three ways to change a habit Change the shape. If you always write lists, tell one short story. If you always tell stories, write a checklist. Change the angle. Write about what went wrong, not what went right. Or argue with an idea everyone in your field repeats. Change the format. If you always post text, try a document or a poll. More on that next. issue:one-good-prompt Your visuals need work People see the image before they read a word. A blurry photo, a crowded slide or a stock picture that has nothing to do with the text tells them to keep scrolling. LinkedIn gives you more formats than most people use. From the composer you can add a photo or video, an event or a celebration. Under the Plus icon you can create a poll, add a document, share that you're hiring, or add Services. Its posting help page lists these. Document posts are worth a look. LinkedIn's documents page says they take PPT, PPTX, DOC, DOCX and PDF files, up to 100MB and 300 pages. Two details to know before you upload: after posting, you can edit the description but not the document itself people who can…

title: Free, and enough.
subtitle: Seven jobs, seven free AI tools, and exactly where each free plan stops:
text: You don't need to pay for AI to start using it at work. You need to know which free plan does which job. And where each one stops. Most "best free AI tools" lists skip that last part. Then you hit a wall in the middle of a task. I teach people to use AI at work. So this issue sticks to one rule: Every limit below comes from the vendor's own pricing or help page. No guesses, no reviews, no rumours. Pages were read on 27 November 2026, on US pages. Plans change often, and features vary by country, so check the link before you rely on a detail. Inside, one free tool per job: Everyday chat: ChatGPT Free Writing and documents: Claude Free Research and search: Perplexity Free Slides: Gamma Free Images: Gemini Meeting notes: Otter Basic Coding: GitHub Copilot Free Each one comes with a prompt to copy and the limit to watch. Think and write Three jobs most people do every day: ask, write and look things up. One free tool for each. 1. Everyday chat: ChatGPT Free For quick questions, rewording an email, explaining a term: ChatGPT's free plan is the most generous on volume. OpenAI's pricing page advertises unlimited text chats with GPT-6 on Free, subject to abuse guardrails. What Free limits, in OpenAI's words: uploads, image creation, voice chats, deep research, and memory and context are all "limited". Two more things to know: Short memory per chat. The context window on Free is 27K tokens with GPT Instant. Plus has 54K. Long documents won't fit in one go. Ads. OpenAI says ads may appear for Free and Go users. Paid plans from Plus up have none. Rewrite this email so it's shorter and friendlier, but keeps every date and number exactly as written. Then give me a subject line of six words or fewer. [paste your email] Prefer Microsoft? It also offers a limited free version of Copilot, subject to available capacity. When you hit a limit, you upgrade or come back later. ChatGPT's plans · OpenAI on ads 2. Writing and documents: Claude Free When you need a proper document, a report or a one-pager, use Claude's free plan. Claude's pricing page lists a lot on Free: chat on web, desktop and mobile, web search, file creation and code, memory, connectors, Artifacts, and Claude Design, Slides and Docs. It can hand you a real file. Claude creates Word, PowerPoint, Excel and PDF files in the conversation, and file creation is on by default for Free. Anthropic has also committed that Claude will stay ad-free. What Free limits: Usage. Limited usage every 5 hours and every week. The number of messages varies with demand. Models. Sonnet and Haiku only. Opus and Fable are on paid plans. Apps. Chat works on Free. Claude Code and Cowork need a paid plan. Projects. Up to five. Sharing. Claude's help centre shows link sharing for new artifacts on paid plans, not Free. Turn the notes below into a one-page Word document for my manager. Structure: a two-line summary, then three sections (what happened, what it means, what I recommend), then a short list of next steps with owners. Plain English. No jargon. Keep every number exactly as in my notes. [paste your notes] Claude's plans 3. Research and search: Perplexity Free For questions where you want sources, start with Perplexity. Its help centre says Free gives practically unlimited basic searches. What Free limits: 3 Pro Searches a day 1 Research query a month limited file uploads no advanced AI models and no image generation So save the one monthly Research query for the question that really matters. What changed in [your topic] in the last 12 months? Give me five points, each with the source it comes from. Then tell me which two points the sources disagree on. Need a longer report? Google's free Gemini plan includes Deep Research too. Google AI Plus gives twice the usage of Free, and AI Pro four times. Google's free plan also includes Gemini Notebook, the name Google's plans page now uses for NotebookLM. It's listed as a "research and writing assistant". Paid plans add more notebooks and Audio Overviews. Perplexity's plans guide:claude-from-zero Make things Two jobs that used to need a designer: a deck and a picture. 4. Slides: Gamma Free Gamma turns a prompt into a presentation. Its free plan is a good way to get a first draft of a deck. Gamma's help centre says Free includes AI creations, the AI Agent, basic image models, up to 10 slides per prompt and 50k input tokens. The catch is credits: Every AI action uses credits: presentations, images and AI-agent edits. Free credits don't refresh. When they're gone, they're gone. You earn 200 credits per referral and can hold up to 2,000. Two more limits worth knowing. Removing the "Made with Gamma" badge from what you share or export is a Plus feature. So is going past 10 slides per prompt (Plus allows up to 100). Make a 10-slide presentation for my team about [topic]. Audience: busy colleagues who haven't seen this before. Slide 1: the one-sentence point. Slides 2 to 8: one idea each, a short headline and three bullets. Slide 9: the decision we need. Slide 10: next steps with owners. Keep the words short. No more than 25 words per slide. Since credits don't come back, write the prompt properly the first time. A clear outline costs the same credits as a vague one. Already on Claude? Its free plan lists Slides too, and a deck made from a template exports to PowerPoint, PDF or Google Slides. Gamma's plans 5. Images: Gemini For pictures, use Google's Gemini app. Google says the Nano Banana 2 image model is free in the Gemini app: it makes and edits images at 2K resolution. Its best image model, Nano Banana 2.1, needs a paid Google AI plan, which also gives higher image limits. How to make one: Open the Gemini app and open the tools menu. Select Create images. Type your prompt, or upload an image you want to edit. Good to know: Every Gemini image carries a visible watermark and an invisible SynthID watermark. It can put clear text inside an image, in many languages. You can upload any image to Gemini and ask whether Google AI…

title: Hand Claude the mouse.
subtitle: Let Claude click, type and open apps for you, with the safety settings that matter, in six steps:
text: Some jobs live inside an app. No connector reaches them. No upload helps. Someone has to open the app, click, type, copy, paste. Until now, that someone was you. Claude can now do it. It can see your screen, click, type and open apps on your computer. Anthropic calls it computer use. It's useful. It's also the most powerful thing you can switch on in Claude. So it deserves a careful set-up. I teach people to use AI at work, and this is the set-up to get right first. Inside: Check you have what it needs Switch it on Choose how much Claude asks first Allow apps one at a time Run a small first task Put a task on a schedule Plus five everyday jobs with prompts you can copy. Why let Claude click for you Claude always reaches for the most precise tool first. If a connector can do the job, it uses the connector. If not, the browser. Only then does it work on your screen directly. So computer use is the fallback for everything else: the desktop app with no connector, the old system nobody built a link to, the file that only opens in one program. That's what it saves you. The clicking between apps. Two honest limits before you start: Working on the screen is slower than a connector. Complex tasks sometimes need a second try. Good to know before you judge it on day one. New to Cowork? Start here Step 1: Check you have what it needs Computer use runs through Claude Desktop, the app you install on your computer. Here's what the help pages say you need: What you need Plan Pro, Max or Ultra. On Team and Enterprise it's a beta that an owner must turn on first. Computer A Mac (computer use needs macOS 14 or later) or a Windows PC (Windows 10 or higher). Not supported Linux. Computer use isn't available there. While it works Your computer awake, Claude Desktop open, and an internet connection. Pro is $20 a month, or $17 a month if you pay yearly. No Claude Desktop yet? Get it from claude.com/download. On Team and Enterprise, there's one more catch. Computer use works only in the new Claude experience. It doesn't work in tasks started with the "Cowork" option, or in Claude Code. How do you know you have the new experience? Your message box no longer shows "Chat" and "Cowork". Your Cowork tasks run on Anthropic's servers, in the cloud. But anything that touches your own screen, your local files or the browser needs Claude Desktop open on your computer. Step 2: Switch it on It's one switch. Open Claude Desktop. Go to Settings → Capabilities. (On some versions it's Settings → System, under "This computer".) Turn on Enable computer use. That's it for the switch. Nothing happens yet. Claude only asks for an app when you give it a task that needs one. On a Mac Claude also needs two macOS permissions: Accessibility and Screen & System Audio Recording. If Claude can't see or click anything, check both are on. Background or full control On macOS 15 or later, Claude works in background windows by default. It doesn't take over your pointer, so you can keep working. If you'd rather it drives the pointer, look for How Claude uses the apps you allow and choose Full control. Start with the default. Step 3: Choose how much Claude asks first Every task has an approval mode. It decides how often Claude stops to check with you. Mode What happens Use it when Manually approve Claude pauses and you click Allow or Deny You're new to this, or the task touches anything sensitive Automatically approve Claude keeps going, but each action is checked for safety and unsafe ones are blocked Routine work you've already watched it do Skip all approvals Nothing checks Claude's actions Only when you fully trust every app, file and connector involved The older names were "Ask before acting" and "Act without asking", in case you see those. Anthropic is clear that the automatic check can miss risky actions. For anything involving money, messages sent as you or important files, stay close or switch to Manually approve. Cowork normally asks before it permanently deletes a file. That protection does not cover computer use. Keep backups of anything that matters, and don't point Claude at files you can't afford to lose. Step 4: Allow apps one at a time Claude asks your permission before it touches each app. Once you say yes, it can keep using that app for the rest of that session without asking again. Not every app gets the same access: Kind of app What Claude can do Browsers, and many investment, trading and crypto apps Look only Terminals and code editors Click and scroll, but not type Most other apps Full access Music, video streaming and e-book apps Nothing: they're off limits You can also block apps yourself. Claude's requests for a blocked app are denied automatically. What not to allow Anthropic recommends you don't give computer use access to sensitive apps: banking, healthcare, government. Treat that as a hard rule, not a suggestion. Two things that surprise people It can reach beyond your folders. In Cowork, Claude normally works only in the folders you connect. Computer use isn't limited that way. Links can open other apps. If Claude clicks a link inside an app you approved, that can open another app, Chrome for example, even though you never approved Chrome. Both are good reasons to start small. issue:check-a-skill-before-you-trust-it Step 5: Run a small first task Pick one app. One small job. Something you could check in a minute. Use Manually approve, and watch. If you have the "Cowork" option in your message box, select it first. If you have the new Claude experience, just type the task into any conversation. Open [app name] on my computer. Find [the item, e.g. last week's report] and tell me [what you want to know, e.g. the total in the last row]. Rules: - Only use [app name]. Ask me before opening anything else. - Don't change, move, send or delete anything. - If you get stuck, stop and tell me what you see. Claude will ask to use the app. Allow it. Then follow along. Read each step before you click Allow. How to know it worked…

title: Claude is a toolkit.
subtitle: Six tools in one app, and how to set each one up:
text: You open Claude. You ask a question. You copy the answer somewhere else. That's one tool. Claude has at least six. Set each one up once, and Claude stops being a tab you visit. It becomes the place you work. I teach people to use AI at work. This is the set-up I'd want every one of them to have. Here's each tool, with when to reach for it, a first prompt and one tip: The model menu, for the right model and effort Projects, for work that keeps coming back Artifacts, for work you'll put in front of someone Plugins and skills, for a set-up that fits your role Cowork, for tasks with several steps Claude for Excel, for work that lives in a spreadsheet Where to double-check Claude A set-up you can finish in half an hour Pick the model, then the effort The model menu next to the send button holds several Claude models. Each one has a job: Model Reach for it when Speed Opus 5.5 Most of your work. Anthropic calls it the "strongest daily driver" Moderate Fable 5.2 Hard reasoning, and long tasks with many steps Moderate Sonnet 5.5 Everyday tasks, and polished documents, slides and spreadsheets Fast Haiku 5.5 Lots of quick, simple jobs Fastest On Free, you get Sonnet and Haiku. Opus is on Pro, Max and Ultra. Fable is on paid plans, though on Pro it runs on usage credits. When to switch: start on Opus 5.5, as Anthropic's own docs advise when you're unsure. Move up or down only when the job asks for it. Where to find it: click the model name next to the send button and pick a model, or click More models. On your phone, the model name sits at the top of the screen. Then set the effort. Click the model name, click Effort and choose Low, Medium, High, Extra high or Max. The level Anthropic recommends for each model is marked Default. A first prompt to copy: run one real task on two models, then compare. Here's an update I need to send my manager: [paste it]. Rewrite it so the decision we need comes first, then the three facts behind it. Keep it under ten lines. Send it on Sonnet 5.5. Then switch to Opus 5.5 and send it again. The switch applies from Claude's next answer. On Free, compare Sonnet with Haiku. What you get back: two versions of the same update. Keep the model whose answer you'd send without edits. Still picking Sonnet 4.6? It leaves the model menu on Free, Pro, Max and Ultra on December 8, 2026. Anthropic recommends Sonnet 5.5 instead. Leave effort on Default until you have a reason to change it. Higher effort takes longer and uses more of your limits, so save it for work that needs careful thinking. issue:opus-5-5 Projects, for work that comes back Some work isn't a one-off. A client. A course. The report you write every month. A project gives that work its own space: its own chats, its own files and its own instructions. Claude keeps a separate memory for each project, too. Projects are on every plan. Free accounts can make up to five. When to use it: any piece of work you return to, with files you'd otherwise upload again and again. Where to find it: Click Projects on the left, or go to claude.ai/projects. Click + New Project in the top right and name it. Claude doesn't see the name or description, so save instructions for step 4. In the project's knowledge, on the right, click + and add your files. Click Set project instructions, write how Claude should work here, then Save instructions. A first prompt to copy, in a new chat inside the project: Using only the files and instructions in this project, tell me in five lines what this piece of work is about. Then list what's missing that you'd need to do it well, and ask me for it. What you get back: a short summary, and a list of the gaps to fill before the real work starts. Chats in a project don't share context with each other. If something matters to every chat, add it to the project's knowledge. Keep the files you use again and again in the project, not in each chat. Project content is cached, so it counts less against your usage limits when you reuse it. Skill, project or instructions? How to choose Artifacts, for work you'll share Some answers you read once. Others you send. For the second kind, Claude makes an artifact: a document, deck, design, dashboard or small interactive tool that opens beside the chat. You can edit it, come back to it and share it. Artifacts are on every plan, including the Docs, Slides and Design templates. When to use it: whenever the result is something you'll send, present or reuse. Where to find it: ask for one in any chat. Or select Output in the message box and choose a template. Everything you make is saved in the Artifacts tab in the sidebar. Artifacts need Create and edit files switched on in Settings → Capabilities. It's on by default on Free, Pro, Max and Ultra. A first prompt to copy: Turn the notes below into a one-page doc for my manager: the decision we need, three options with the cost and risk of each, and my recommendation. Plain English, no jargon. [paste your notes] What you get back: a doc beside the chat. Start it from the Docs template and you can type in it directly, then export it to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs. Decks made with Slides export to PowerPoint or PDF. Don't describe which paragraph to fix. Highlight it, click Edit with Claude and type the change. Claude edits right where you marked. Get the next issue by email Plugins and skills, for your role Out of the box, Claude is a generalist. Plugins and skills fit it to your work. Plugins bundle skills, connectors and sub-agents into one package, so you get a ready-made set-up for your role from the first conversation. The library covers sales, finance, legal, marketing, HR, engineering, design, operations, data analysis and more. Plugins are on paid plans. Skills are folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads when a task needs them. They're on every plan. Claude already has built-in skills for Excel, Word, PowerPoint and PDF files, and uses them by itself. Connectors let Claude reach your other apps and…

title: The one line Claude reads.
subtitle: Your Claude skill isn't broken. Its description is. Here's how to write the line Claude uses to choose:
text: You made a Claude skill. You uploaded it. You switched it on. And Claude never uses it. Or worse: it uses it when you didn't ask. You open the instructions. You rewrite the steps. You add examples. Nothing changes. Because the problem isn't in the steps. It's in one line at the top of the file. What's inside: Why one line decides everything What Claude actually sees The two jobs of a description The rules Before and after: three rewrites A prompt that rewrites yours The five-request test Why one line decides everything Claude decides when to use a skill from its description alone. Not the steps. Not the examples. Not the long instructions you wrote below it. That's because skills load in layers: Always: Claude sees just the name and description of every skill you've switched on. A line or two each. When a request matches: it reads that skill's instructions. Only if needed: it opens the extra files. So most of the time, the description is the only part of your skill Claude sees. A great skill with a weak description is a skill Claude never opens. What Claude actually sees Picture your skills the way Claude meets them: a short list of names and descriptions, one or two lines each. Something like this: weekly-report: Turns the week's notes and numbers into our team's weekly report format. Use when someone asks for the weekly report or pastes weekly updates. meeting-notes: Helps with meetings. A request comes in: "Here are this week's updates. Can you write the report?" The first line tells Claude exactly when to step in. The second could mean anything. Your description is competing for attention in that list. Make it impossible to misread. The two jobs of a description A strong description does two things: Says what the skill does. Says when to use it. Most weak descriptions do only the first. The "when" is where you name the trigger: the words or situations that should make Claude reach for it. "When someone asks for the weekly report." "When someone pastes a meeting transcript." The rules Part Rule Voice The third person: "Turns the week's notes...", not "I help you..." Length 200 characters at most in the Claude apps (the API allows 1,024) Format No tags in angle brackets Content What it does and when to use it And one rule from experience: one skill, one job. A description that has to explain two jobs is a sign you need two skills. New to skills? Start with the guide Before and after: three rewrites The weekly report Helps with reports. Turns the week's notes and numbers into our team's weekly report format. Use when someone asks for the weekly report or pastes weekly updates. Meeting notes I help you with your meetings. Turns meeting notes or a transcript into decisions, actions with owners and deadlines, and a follow-up email. Use when someone pastes meeting notes or a transcript. Learning a topic A tutor skill for learning things and also making quizzes. Teaches any topic step by step, starting from what the learner already knows. Use when someone asks to learn, understand or be taught a topic. Notice what changed each time. Third person. One job. A clear trigger. And the quiz part moved out: that's a second skill. Get the next issue by email A prompt that rewrites yours Have a skill already? Paste its SKILL.md into a normal chat with this: Here is my skill's SKILL.md. Rewrite its description so it says what the skill does and when to use it, in the third person, in 200 characters or fewer, with no tags in angle brackets. Then give me three requests that should use the skill and two that shouldn't. [paste your SKILL.md here] Read what comes back. Keep it only if it's true to how you work. You'll find more prompts like this in the library. The five-request test A new description isn't done until it passes this: Write three requests that should use the skill. Write two that shouldn't. Upload the skill, switch it on, and try all five. All three "should" requests used the skill Neither "shouldn't" request did Claude missed one? Don't touch the steps. Rewrite the description first. Still ignored? Check that the skill's switch is on in Customize → Skills, and name it in your request: "Use my weekly-report skill on these notes." What to do today Open your skills. Read each description out loud. Does it say what and when? If not, run the prompt above, then the five-request test. Ten minutes per skill. Then Claude uses them when it should, and only then. issue:make-your-first-skill Send this to one person whose skill never gets used. Mojeed

title: Check a skill before you trust it.
subtitle: A Claude skill can run code on your behalf. Here's what can go wrong, and the five-minute check to run first:
text: A colleague sends you a skill. "This one is great. It does our weekly reports." You download the zip. You upload it. You switch it on. It works. Everyone's happy. But you just let someone else's code run inside your Claude, with access to whatever you give it. Most skills are harmless. Some aren't. The good news: checking a skill takes about five minutes, and you don't need to be technical. Here's everything: Why a skill is more than a prompt The two real risks The five-minute check, step by step What a script should never do Ask Claude to review a skill for you What teams and companies can turn on What to do if something looks wrong Why a skill is more than a prompt A prompt is words. You read it before you send it. A skill can be more than that. Besides the SKILL.md file, a skill can carry: reference files that Claude reads when it needs them templates it fills in scripts: code that runs when Claude uses the skill And here's the part most people miss: skills load in layers. Claude reads the instructions only when a request matches, and opens the extra files only if needed. Scripts run, and only their results come back to Claude. So you might use a skill for weeks without ever seeing what's inside. Treat an unknown skill like an unknown app. You wouldn't install an app from a stranger without a second look. The two real risks 1. Prompt injection Hidden instructions that steer Claude into something you didn't ask for. They can hide anywhere in a skill's text: deep in the instructions, in a reference file, in a template. You ask for your weekly report. The skill quietly tells Claude to do something else as well. 2. Data leaks A script that sends your information somewhere. Your notes, your numbers, your files: whatever you give the skill to work on. Anthropic's advice for both risks is the same: check before you trust. The five-minute check Do this before you upload any skill you didn't write yourself. Step 1: The source (30 seconds) Who made it? Install only from sources you trust. Even a skill a colleague shares deserves a look first. They may not have checked it either. Don't know the source? Stop here. Step 2: Read SKILL.md (2 minutes) Unzip a copy of the skill on your computer. Open SKILL.md. Read it from top to bottom. Ask yourself: Does the description match the job it promises? Do the instructions stay on that job? Is there anything that tells Claude to do something unrelated, or to hide what it's doing? Step 3: Read every script (2 minutes) Look in the scripts/ folder, if there is one. You don't need to understand every line. You're looking for two things: anything that downloads software anything that sends information to a website If you see a web address in a script, ask why it's there. Step 4: Look for secrets (30 seconds) There should be no passwords, API keys or personal data in a skill. Not in the instructions, not in a file. If you find one, the skill was built carelessly. That's reason enough to stop. Step 5: Test it on something harmless Upload it. Switch it on. Try it first on files that don't matter. Does it do what it says, and only that? Then you can use it for real work. Save the full skills guide What a script should never do Scripts are useful. They're the right tool for steps that must come out the same every time: calculations, format checks, conversions. But a script for those jobs has no reason to: download software send information to a website read files you didn't give it contain passwords or keys A script that formats a report doesn't need the internet. If it reaches out to a website, ask why before you switch the skill on. Here's a useful comparison. Every skill in the library I wrote for the people I teach is plain text you can read in a minute. Only three files are scripts, and they use only Python's standard library and never connect to the internet. That's the bar. Hold every skill to it. Get the next issue by email Ask Claude to review a skill for you Not comfortable reading code? Let Claude help. Paste the skill's files into a normal chat, with the skill switched off, and ask: I'm about to install this Claude skill. Read every file below and tell me, in plain English: 1. What the skill does. 2. Whether any instruction asks for something unrelated to that job, or hides what it's doing. 3. Whether any script downloads software, sends information to a website, or reads files it wasn't given. 4. Whether there are passwords, API keys or personal data anywhere. Quote the exact lines you're worried about. [paste the files here] Read the answer carefully. Then look at the lines it quotes yourself. This helps, but it doesn't replace your own read of the files. Hidden instructions are written to be missed. What teams and companies can turn on If your company uses Claude on a team plan, there's more you can do. Team plans: skills are on by default, so it's worth agreeing as a team which skills you trust. Enterprise plans: an owner turns skills on first, in Organization settings → Plugins & skills, on the Policy tab. Skill scanning: on Enterprise plans, owners can turn on skill scanning, which checks uploaded skills for malicious content. Keep a short shared list of the skills your team has checked, and who checked them. It saves everyone from repeating the work. If something looks wrong Don't switch it on. Already did? Open Customize → Skills and switch it off. Then: Tell whoever shared it what you found. Delete the zip from wherever you saved it. If you gave it files with personal or company data, tell the person responsible for security at your company. There's no shame in it. Checking is exactly what you're supposed to do. Questions people ask Do I need to check skills I wrote myself? Less so. But re-read anything you copied in from elsewhere: an example, a template or a script you found online. What about skills in Claude's own directory? In Customize → Skills → + → Browse skills, you'll find skills from partners such as Notion, Figma and Atlassian…

title: Ten skills worth writing.
subtitle: The ten Claude skills I wrote for the people I teach: what each one does, why it works, and a request to try:
text: People ask me the same question every week. "I get what a skill is. But what should I actually make one for?" So here's my answer, in full. These are the ten skills I wrote for the people I teach. Each one does one job, the way I'd want it done. I'll show you what each does, the rules that make it work, and a request to try. Steal the ideas. Then write your own versions, for the way you work. What's inside: Two skills for learning Two for research Two for your career Two for everyday work One for data One that writes the others How to choose your first The ten, on one page Every skill below follows the same pattern. A clear job. A few firm rules. One thing it never does. That last part matters most. A good skill isn't only what Claude does. It's what Claude refuses to do. Learn and remember learn-anything A patient tutor for any topic. It doesn't start explaining right away. First it asks what you already know. Then it makes a short plan, and explains one idea at a time, each with an analogy and a small example. Before moving on, it checks you understood. Why it works: most explanations start in the wrong place. Too basic, and you're bored. Too advanced, and you're lost. Asking first fixes both. Teach me how neural networks learn. I know basic algebra. Always say what you already know. "I know basic algebra" changes the whole explanation. quiz-me Turns your notes, a document or a topic into practice questions. It asks them one at a time. It explains every answer, keeps track of what you miss, and comes back to it. Why it works: reading notes feels like learning. Answering questions is learning. And coming back to the ones you missed is where it sticks. Quiz me on these lecture notes. Ten questions, mixed. Make your own version: the five steps Research and explain research-brief Answers a question with a one-page, sourced brief. It separates what's known from what's only claimed. It gives each finding a confidence level. And it never invents a source. Why it works: the danger with AI research isn't a wrong answer. It's a wrong answer that sounds certain. Confidence levels and real sources make the uncertainty visible. news-explainer Turns AI and tech news into a plain explainer, in four parts: What happened Why it matters Who it affects What's still unknown Every claim is attributed. No hype. Why it works: the fourth part. Most news coverage skips what isn't known yet. Naming it keeps you honest with your readers. Explain this announcement for my newsletter readers. Paste the link or the text under it. Grow your career linkedin-post Writes LinkedIn posts in your own voice, from an idea, a lesson or a piece of work. You get an opening worth reading and one clear point. What you don't get: invented stories or engagement bait. Why it works: it learns your voice from your own old posts. So the post sounds like you on a good day, not like a template. Turn this project I finished into a post. Here are two of my old posts. job-application Tailors your CV and cover letter to one specific job ad. It matches your real experience to what the employer asks for. And it tells you honestly where the gaps are. Why it works: honesty. A tailored CV that invents experience falls apart in the interview. One that tells you where you're weak gives you time to prepare. Here's my CV and the job ad. Tailor both. Get the next issue by email Get work done meeting-to-actions Turns meeting notes or a transcript into: the decisions the actions, with owners and deadlines the open questions a follow-up email, ready to send It never invents an owner or a date. Why it works: a summary nobody acts on is wasted. Owners and deadlines turn a meeting into work that gets done. And refusing to invent them means you find the gaps before they cost you. Here's the transcript of today's team call. presentation-planner Plans a talk before you open slide software: the story one message per slide titles that state the point the visuals the speaker notes Why it works: most bad decks are a planning problem, not a design problem. Fix the story first, and the slides almost write themselves. Plan a ten-minute talk on our quarterly results for the board. Work with data check-the-numbers Answers questions about spreadsheets, CSV files and SQL results, and proves the answer first. A script profiles each file before Claude answers: missing values numbers stored as text repeated rows and keys gaps in the dates Every join is checked for multiplied rows. And the answer comes with its caveats. Why it works: this is the skill where a script earns its place. Checking data must come out the same every time, and code does that better than words. Which products drove last quarter's revenue? Here's the export. When a step must be exact (a calculation, a format check, a conversion), put it in a script, not in the instructions. Make your own skill-maker The one that writes the others. It interviews you about a task you repeat. Then it writes the SKILL.md, checks it against the rules, and packages the folder as a zip, ready to upload. Why it works: the hardest part of a skill is describing your own job. Being interviewed is much easier than starting from a blank page. Help me turn the way I write our weekly report into a skill. The full walkthrough: make your first skill What a good skill looks like inside Every skill above is the same shape inside: a name, a description, and short, firm instructions. Here's how learn-anything could look, so you can see the pattern: --- name: learn-anything description: Teaches any topic step by step, starting from what the learner already knows. Use when someone asks to learn, understand or be taught a topic. --- ## Steps 1. Ask what I already know about the topic, and why I want to learn it. 2. Make a short plan: three to five ideas, in order. 3. Explain one idea at a time, with an analogy and a small example. 4. Ask one question to check I understood before moving on. ## Mistakes to avoid - Don't explain everything in…

title: Make your first skill.
subtitle: Turn the instructions you paste into Claude every day into a skill that does the job your way:
text: Every morning, the same ritual. You open Claude. You paste the same long block of instructions. You explain the format again. The tone. The headings. The thing it got wrong yesterday. Then you correct the same mistakes. There's a better way, and it takes about an hour, once. You teach Claude the job one time, in a skill. From then on, Claude picks it up by itself whenever a request needs it. No pasting. No re-explaining. Your way, every time. Here's everything you need to make your first one: Know when a task deserves a skill Pick the right first task Understand what's inside a skill Write the SKILL.md, and the line that matters most Write the instructions Add templates and scripts (only if you need them) Zip it the right way Upload it and test it with five requests Fix it when Claude doesn't use it Know when a task deserves a skill Not everything should be a skill. Claude already gives you three other ways to shape how it works. Each one fits a different need: Custom instructions hold your general preferences. They apply to every conversation. Projects hold background documents and knowledge. They apply to the chats inside that project. Connectors give Claude access to other apps and data, such as your drive or calendar, when it needs them. A skill is a way of doing one particular job. It applies only when a request needs it, in any chat. My rule is simple. Once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times, make it a skill. Once is a one-off. Twice is a coincidence. Three times is a job, and jobs deserve skills. Skills and connectors work well together. A connector lets Claude reach your project tracker; a skill teaches it how your team writes tickets. Not sure what a skill is? Start with the guide Pick the right first task Your first skill should be boring. That's a compliment. Boring jobs are the ones you repeat, and the ones you repeat are where a skill pays off fastest. Good first tasks The weekly report your manager expects in a fixed format. The summary you write after every client meeting. The email you send in your team's tone, again and again. The checklist you run before you send anything important. Tasks to leave for later A job you do once a quarter. You won't remember to use it. A job that is really three jobs. Split it, or the skill will do all three badly. A job you can't describe yet. If you can't explain it to a colleague, you can't explain it to Claude. One skill, one job. If you need two jobs, make two skills. Throughout this issue, I'll use one example: a weekly report. Understand what's inside a skill A skill is just a folder. It has one required file, SKILL.md, and a few optional ones: weekly-report/ ├── SKILL.md required: name, description and instructions ├── reference.md optional: detail Claude reads only when it needs it ├── templates/ optional: files to fill in └── scripts/ optional: code for steps that must be exact That's the whole thing. No app to build. No code to write, unless you want to. Why you can have many skills Skills load in layers. Always: Claude sees just the name and description of every skill you've switched on. A line or two each. When a request matches: Claude reads that skill's instructions. Only if needed: it opens the extra files. Scripts run, and only their results come back. So ten skills don't slow Claude down. Each one costs a line or two until the moment it's needed. This is also why the description matters so much. Most of the time, it's the only part of your skill Claude sees. Write the SKILL.md Make a folder named after your skill: weekly-report. Inside it, make a file called SKILL.md. It starts with a name and a description, between two lines of dashes: --- name: weekly-report description: Turns the week's notes and numbers into our team's weekly report format. Use when someone asks for the weekly report or pastes weekly updates. --- The name Lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only. 64 characters at most. The same as the folder's name. It can't contain "claude" or "anthropic". The name is also the command you can type, like /weekly-report. The description: the line that matters most Claude decides when to use your skill from the description alone. Write it badly, and your skill sits there unused. Write it well, and Claude reaches for it at the right moment, every time. A strong description does two things: Says what the skill does. Says when to use it. Write it in the third person ("Turns the week's notes...", not "I help you..."). Keep it to 200 characters in the Claude apps (the API allows 1,024). No tags in angle brackets. Compare these two: Helps with reports. Turns the week's notes and numbers into our team's weekly report format. Use when someone asks for the weekly report or pastes weekly updates. The first one could mean anything. The second one tells Claude exactly when to step in. Get the next guide by email Write the instructions Below the dashes comes the job itself. Write it the way you'd brief a sharp new colleague on their first day. Keep it under 500 lines, and include four things: Numbered steps. What to do, in order. The mistakes to avoid. The ones Claude made last time. One short example. A good finished result. A checklist, if the job is long. Here's how the weekly report skill could start: ## Steps 1. Read the notes and numbers I paste. 2. Group them under: Wins, Numbers, Risks, Next week. 3. Keep each point to one line. 4. Put the three numbers that changed most at the top of Numbers. ## Mistakes to avoid - Don't invent numbers. If one is missing, write [missing]. - Don't add a greeting or a sign-off. ## Example (paste one report you were happy with) Your best example is a real one. Paste a report you were proud of, with anything private removed. Let Claude draft it with you Don't want to start from a blank page? Ask Claude to interview you first: Help me turn the way I write our weekly report into a skill. Ask me questions first, then write the SKILL.md. Answer its questions honestly. Then…

title: Ask Claude about your data, and trust the answer.
subtitle: Claude will answer any question about your spreadsheet, confidently. Here's how to make sure the answer is right:
text: You upload a spreadsheet. You ask Claude a question. You get a clear, confident answer, with a number in bold. And sometimes that number is wrong. Not because Claude can't count. Because nobody told it what the data means, and nobody checked the working. In data work, this is the same problem we've always had with reports: a confident number is not a correct number. The fix is the same too. You prepare the data, define your terms and check the working. By the end of this guide you'll have: a file Claude can read without guessing a prompt that makes Claude describe the data before it answers a simple way to check any number in two minutes You need: a spreadsheet or CSV file, and ten minutes. 1. Know why confident answers go wrong Claude writes every answer in the same calm, clear voice. A correct answer and a wrong one sound exactly alike. Most wrong answers about data come from four places: The file is messy. A totals row at the bottom gets counted as a sale. Two tables sit on one sheet. The question is vague. "Revenue" could mean before or after refunds. "Last quarter" could mean calendar or financial. Nobody looked at the working. The answer came back, and nobody asked how it was worked out. Nobody checked. One number, taken on trust, goes into a slide. Each step below fixes one of them. Treat Claude like a sharp new analyst on their first day. Brilliant, fast, and new to your data. You'd brief them and check their first report. Do the same here. 2. Prepare the file in two minutes Clean files get correct answers.
