Before you upload: One header row at the top, with a clear name for every column. One table per sheet. Move notes, charts and side tables to another sheet. Delete totals and subtotal rows. Claude can add up. A totals row gets counted twice. One format per column. Dates all written the same way. Numbers without text like "approx." or "n/a". Remove what's private. Names, emails and phone numbers usually aren't needed to answer the question. Replace them with an ID. If Claude says it can't open the file, check Settings → Capabilities and turn on Create and edit files. Don't upload customer or staff data your company hasn't cleared for AI tools. Ask first. Anonymised data answers most questions just as well. 3. Make Claude describe the data first This is the step that changes everything. Before you ask your real question, ask Claude to tell you what it sees: Before answering anything, describe this file: 1. How many rows and columns, and what each column contains. 2. The date range. 3. Missing values, numbers stored as text, and repeated rows. 4. Anything that looks like a totals row or a second table. Don't analyse anything yet. Read the answer like a checklist. Does the row count match what you expect? Is the date range right? Did it find the totals row you forgot to delete? If something's off, fix the file and upload it again. It takes a minute now, and saves a wrong number later. 4. Define your terms Vague questions get confident guesses. Say exactly what you mean: Which column? "Use the Net_Amount column, not Gross." Which rows? "Leave out cancelled orders (Status = Cancelled)." Which dates? "Last quarter means July to September 2026." Which unit? "Show revenue in thousands of pounds, rounded." Compare these two: Which product made the most money last quarter? Which product had the highest revenue from July to September 2026? Use the Net_Amount column and leave out rows where Status is Cancelled. Show the top five, with their revenue. The first one makes Claude guess three things. The second one leaves nothing to guess. 5. Ask for the working, not just the answer A number without the working is a number you can't check. Ask Claude to show: the steps it took, in order the row count after each step ("after removing cancelled orders: 4,812 rows") the formula or code it used, so you can run it again Show your working: list each step, the number of rows after each step, and the formula you used. Then give the answer. Row counts are your best friend. If 4,812 rows suddenly become 9,624 after combining two tables, something has gone wrong, and you'll see it straight away. 6. Check it two ways You don't need to redo the analysis. You need two quick checks. Ask for the same number another way. "Now calculate the same total with a pivot table instead of a formula. Do they match?" Spot-check three rows by hand. Pick three rows from the file and see if they were counted the way you expected. And one sanity check: does the answer fit what you already know? If last quarter's total revenue was about two million, a product earning three million is a red flag. Ask Claude to check itself: "What could make this answer wrong? List the three most likely problems with the data or the method." It's surprisingly good at finding its own weak spots once you ask. 7. Watch for the five traps These cause most wrong answers. Ask Claude to check for each one. Numbers stored as text "1,200" typed as text doesn't add up. It gets skipped, or sorted in the wrong order. Repeated rows The same order exported twice doubles its revenue. Ask: "Are there repeated rows or repeated order IDs?" Totals counted twice A subtotal row in the middle of the data gets added to the total. Delete them before uploading. Gaps in the dates A missing week looks like a sales drop. Ask: "Are there gaps in the dates?" Joins that multiply rows Combining two tables (orders and customers, say) can copy rows when a key appears more than once. Ask for the row count before and after every join. 8. Put it together Here's the full prompt I'd use for any important question: Here's our sales export. 1. First, describe the file: rows, columns, date range, missing values, numbers stored as text, repeated rows, and any totals rows. 2. Then answer: which product had the highest revenue from July to September 2026? Use Net_Amount and leave out rows where Status is Cancelled. Show the top five. 3. Show your working: each step, the row count after…

title: Brief Claude like a new colleague.
subtitle: Short prompts get average answers. A two-minute brief gets the finished thing, first time:
text: Imagine your manager walks past your desk and says: "Write me a report on sales." Then walks off. You'd have questions. Which sales? For whom? How long? By when? What's it for? Claude has the same questions. It just doesn't ask them. It guesses, and gives you something average. The fix isn't a magic phrase. It's a brief: the same two minutes of context you'd give a sharp new colleague on their first day. By the end of this guide you'll have: the five parts every good brief has a way to get Claude to ask you the questions first a habit that turns three rounds of fixes into one You need: Claude, and one task you'd normally describe in a single line. 1. Know why short prompts get average answers A one-line prompt leaves Claude to fill in everything you didn't say. So it picks the most likely answer. The safe, middle-of-the-road version that would suit anyone. That's why the result often feels generic. It is generic. It was written for nobody in particular, because Claude didn't know who it was for. Every detail you add replaces a guess with a fact. Claude doesn't need clever wording. It needs the information a colleague would need. 2. Use the five parts A good brief answers five questions. You don't need headings, but you do need the answers. The goal: what is this for? Not the task. The reason behind it. "Write a report on sales" is a task. "Help the board decide whether to keep selling in Ghana" is a goal. The second tells Claude what matters and what to leave out. The background: what does Claude need to know? Who's it for, and what do they already know? What happened before? What's been tried? "The board meets on Friday. They've seen last quarter's numbers. Two members think we should pull out." The material: what should it work from? Paste or attach it: the notes, the numbers, the draft, the email thread. Claude can't use what it can't see. If it has to invent the facts, the answer is only as good as its guesses. The shape: what should the answer look like? Length, format, tone and order. "One page. Three options, each with the main risk. Plain English, no jargon. Recommendation at the top." The finish line: when is it done? Say what "done" means, and what Claude should check before it stops. "Done when every number comes from the attached sheet and each option has a cost. If something's missing, list it at the end instead of guessing." 3. Put it together Compare these two: Write me a report on our Ghana sales. Help the board decide whether to keep selling in Ghana. They meet on Friday, have seen last quarter's numbers, and two members want to pull out. Work only from the attached sales sheet and the notes below. Write one page: three options (stay, shrink, pull out), each with its cost and main risk, and your recommendation at the top. Plain English. You're done when every number comes from the sheet. If anything's missing, list it at the end instead of guessing. [notes] The second one takes two minutes longer to write. It saves the three rounds of "no, not like that" that come after the first one. 4. Let Claude ask you first Don't know what to put in the brief? Make Claude interview you. Before you start, ask me the five questions you most need answered to do this well. Wait for my answers. Add it to the end of any request. You'll often find the questions are better than the brief you would have written. This works especially well for big jobs: a strategy, a proposal, a hard email. The questions make you think about what you actually want. 5. Show it what good looks like The fastest way to describe a style is to show it. Paste a past report you were happy with: "Match this format." Paste an email in your tone: "Write like this." Paste a bad example too: "Not like this, it's too formal." One example beats a paragraph of adjectives like "professional but friendly". 6. Correct it like feedback, not a fresh start The first answer is a draft. Treat it like a colleague's draft. Don't start a new chat and rewrite the prompt. Tell Claude what to change, and why: "Shorter. The board reads this on their phones." "Option two is too vague. Give it a real cost." "Keep the structure, but lead with the risk." The why matters. "Shorter" fixes this answer. "Shorter, because they read it on their phones" fixes every answer after it. 7. Save the briefs you reuse Writing the same brief every week? Don't. Context you always need (who you are, how you like things) goes into custom instructions. Background for one piece of work goes into a project. A job you do the same way every time becomes a skill. Not sure which one? This guide picks the right one in two questions: guide:skill-or-something-else Before you finish Your brief says what the work is for, not just what it is. It gives the background a colleague would need. The material is pasted or attached. It describes the shape: length, format, tone. It says when the work is done, and what to do if something's missing. Questions Isn't this a lot of typing? Two minutes. Less than the time you'd spend fixing a generic answer. And once you've written a brief you reuse, you can save it. Do I still need phrases like "act as an expert"? Rarely. A role-play line adds little on its own. The goal, the background and the material do far more. Does this work with other AI tools? Yes. The five parts work with any AI tool, and with any new colleague too.

title: Claude skills, from zero.
subtitle: For anyone who pastes the same instructions into Claude every day: install your first skill safely and use it today.
text: You paste the same long instructions into Claude. You explain the same format again. You correct the same mistakes. A skill ends that. You teach Claude a job once, and it does it your way from then on. By the end of this guide you'll have: one skill installed and switched on a clear idea of when Claude uses it a short safety check you can run on any skill You need: a Claude account and ten minutes. 1. Know what a skill is A skill is a small folder of instructions. Sometimes it also holds scripts and templates. Every skill has one required file: SKILL.md. Its first lines hold two things: a name, which is also the command you can type, such as /learn-anything a description of what the skill does and when to use it Below that come the instructions: steps, rules, examples and checklists. Claude decides when to use a skill from its description alone. A clear description is the difference between a skill that works and one that sits there. 2. See how skills differ You already have other ways to shape Claude. Here's where a skill fits: Feature What it gives Claude When it applies Custom instructions Your general preferences Every conversation Projects Background documents and knowledge Chats inside that project Connectors (MCP) Access to other apps and data When Claude needs that app Skills A way of doing one job Only when a request needs it, in any chat They work well together. A connector lets Claude reach your project tracker. A skill teaches it how your team writes tickets. 3. Check where skills work Skills work in more places than most people think: Claude on the web and in the desktop app, on every plan from Free to Enterprise, once code execution is on. Claude Code, from folders on your computer. Claude for Excel, PowerPoint, Word and Outlook. Cowork, which uses the skills switched on for your account. The Claude API, in beta, where skills run in a sandbox with no internet access. Skills also follow an open standard, the Agent Skills specification. A skill you write isn't locked to one product. 4. Turn skills on Open Settings → Capabilities. Turn on Create and edit files. In the older Settings layout, it's called Code execution and file creation. On Team plans, skills are on by default. On Enterprise plans, an owner turns them on first, in Organization settings → Plugins & skills, on the Policy tab. 5. Install a skill There are two ways to get one. Ready-made: open Customize → Skills, click +, then Browse skills. You'll find skills from partners such as Notion, Figma and Atlassian, built to work with their connectors. From a zip (one you made, or one from a source you trust): Get the skill's zip file. Don't unzip it. Open Customize → Skills, click +, then Create skill → Upload a skill. Choose the zip. Check that the skill's switch is on. That's it. Ask for something the skill covers. Make your own skill 6. Use it You rarely need to do anything special. Claude reads the descriptions of your skills and uses one by itself when your request matches. To be sure, name it: Use my weekly-report skill on these notes. In Claude Code and in the Microsoft 365 add-ins, you can also type / and pick a skill from the list. Claude didn't use the skill you expected? Check that its switch is on, name it in your request, or make its description clearer about when it applies. 7. Add skills to Claude Code Claude Code reads skills from folders on your computer. For every project: unzip the skill into ~/.claude/skills/, so you end up with ~/.claude/skills/learn-anything/SKILL.md. For one project (and everyone who works on it): unzip it into the project's .claude/skills/ folder and commit it. Run a skill by typing a slash and its name, or just ask. /skills lists what's installed. Skills you switch on in your Claude account also sync to Claude Code when you sign in with the same account. Find skills worth installing There are three good places to start. 1. Claude's own directory. In Customize → Skills, click +, then Browse skills. You'll find skills from partners such as Notion, Figma and Atlassian, built to work with their connectors. 2. Anthropic's examples. At github.com/anthropics/skills. Good to learn from, and to adapt to the way you work. 3. Your own. The best skills capture the tasks you repeat every week, the way your organisation does them. Nobody else can write those for you. issue:ten-skills-worth-writing Make your own Once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times, it's worth a skill. The short version: Make a folder named after the job, like weekly-report. Write SKILL.md: a name and a description between two lines of dashes, then numbered steps, the mistakes to avoid and one short example. Zip the folder, not the files inside it. Upload it in Customize → Skills, and switch it on. Test it with three requests that should use it and two that shouldn't. The full walkthrough: make your first skill 8. Stay safe A skill can contain code that runs when Claude uses it. So treat an unknown skill like an unknown app. Never put passwords, API keys or personal data in a skill. The two main risks: Prompt injection: hidden instructions that steer Claude into something you didn't ask for. Data leaks: a script that sends your information somewhere. The fix is the same for both: check before you trust. On Enterprise plans, owners can also turn on skill scanning, which checks uploaded skills for malicious content. Before you finish Create and edit files is on One skill is installed and its switch is on I read every file of that skill before switching it on I asked for something it covers, and Claude used it Questions Do many skills slow Claude down? No. Skills load in layers. Claude always sees just the name and description of each skill you've switched on, a line or two each. It reads the instructions only when a request matches, and extra files only if needed. When is a skill worth making? Once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times. Where can I learn from good examples? Anthropic's…

title: Skill, project, instructions or connector?
subtitle: Claude gives you four ways to teach it how you work. Here's which one to use, and when:
text: You've told Claude how you like things done. Then you told it again, in a new chat. And again the next day. The problem usually isn't Claude. It's that you put the instruction in the wrong place. Claude gives you four ways to shape how it works. Each one applies at a different moment. Pick the right one and you explain things once. By the end of this guide you'll know: what each of the four gives Claude when each one applies, and when it doesn't the two questions that pick the right one in ten seconds 1. The four, side by side Feature What it gives Claude When it applies Custom instructions Your general preferences Every conversation Projects Background documents and knowledge Chats inside that project Connectors (MCP) Access to other apps and data, such as your drive or calendar When Claude needs that app Skills A way of doing one particular job Only when a request needs it, in any chat The last column is the one that matters. It tells you when Claude will remember what you taught it. 2. Custom instructions: how you like things, everywhere Custom instructions hold your general preferences. They apply to every conversation, whatever you're working on. Put here: the things that are true in every chat. How plain you want the language. How long answers should be. The words you never want to see. Don't put here: the steps of one particular job. Those would follow you into every chat, even the ones that have nothing to do with that job. Write in plain English. Keep answers short. Ask me before you assume anything about my work. 3. Projects: the background for one piece of work A project holds background documents and knowledge. It applies only to the chats inside that project. Put here: the files Claude should read for one client, one course or one big piece of work. Open a chat inside the project, and Claude has the background. Don't put here: a way of doing a job you repeat everywhere. The project's chats would know it, and every other chat wouldn't. Using the files here, summarise what changed this month. 4. Connectors: reach into your other apps Connectors give Claude access to other apps and data, such as your drive or calendar. They apply when Claude needs that app. Use them for: anything where the answer lives somewhere else. The latest version of a document. The meetings on your calendar. The tickets in your project tracker. A connector gives Claude access. It doesn't teach Claude how you want a job done. That's the next one. 5. Skills: one job, done your way, in any chat A skill is a way of doing one particular job. It applies only when a request needs it, in any chat. It's a small folder of instructions, and sometimes scripts and templates. Its first lines hold a name and a description. Claude reads the description to decide when to use it. Use them for: the jobs you repeat. The weekly report. The meeting summary. The email in your team's format. Skills load in layers. Claude always sees just the name and description of each skill you've switched on, a line or two each. It reads the instructions only when a request matches. So you can install many without slowing Claude down. My rule: once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times, make it a skill. Make your first skill, step by step 6. Use them together They aren't rivals. They work best together. A connector lets Claude reach your project tracker. A skill teaches it how your team writes tickets. Your custom instructions keep the tone plain. A project holds the background for the work you're tracking. When something keeps going wrong, ask where the fix belongs. A preference for every chat goes in instructions. Background for one piece of work goes in a project. A job you repeat goes in a skill. 7. The two questions Not sure? Ask these, in order. Question 1: Is it a way of doing one particular job? No, and it should apply to every conversation? Custom instructions. No, and it's background for one piece of work? A project. Question 2: Have you explained it to Claude three times? Not yet? Just ask in the chat. Save the prompt you liked. Yes? Make it a skill. Need Claude to reach another app along the way? Add a connector. Before you finish My general preferences are in custom instructions, and nothing job-specific is in there Each big piece of work has its own project with its files The apps Claude needs are connected The job I've explained three times is on my list for a skill Questions Can I use all four at once? Yes. They apply at different moments, so they work together: preferences everywhere, background inside a project, other apps when needed, and a skill when a request needs that job. Will lots of skills slow Claude down? No. Claude sees just a line or two per skill until a request needs one. Where do I start with skills? guide:claude-skills-from-zero

title: Better slides, less effort.
subtitle: Three ways to build a deck with AI, and how your team can share one standard:
text: You have a presentation due. You have the content. Notes, a report, a few numbers. What you don't have is three hours to push boxes around in PowerPoint. AI can do most of that work now. But only if you use it the right way. Ask for "a deck about Q3" and you get ten slides of generic bullets. Give it a real storyline and the right tool, and you get a draft worth editing. I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. This guide is the method I'd show anyone who builds slides for a living, or just once a month. By the end of this guide you'll have: a storyline prompt that makes every method work better method 1: a deck from Claude, as a file, a Slides artifact or inside PowerPoint method 2: a deck from Gamma's agent method 3: the words planned in Claude, the design built in Gamma one standard your whole team can reuse You need: a Claude account (Free works for methods 1 and 3), a Gamma account (Free works to start), and the content for one real presentation. 1. Get the story straight first Most bad AI decks have the same cause. The tool was asked to design and think at the same time. So split the jobs. First decide what the deck says. Then let a tool make it look good. A good storyline answers four questions: Who is in the room? One kind of reader, not "everyone". What should they do after? Approve, decide, learn, buy. What's the one message? If they remember one line, which one? What's the proof? The numbers and examples, each with its source. You don't have to answer these alone. Ask Claude to interview you. I need to build a presentation. Before writing any slides, interview me. Ask me one question at a time about: - who the audience is and what they already know - what I want them to do after the presentation - the one message they should remember - the evidence I have (I'll paste numbers and notes) - how long I have to present When you have enough, give me a storyline: a title, then one line per slide stating that slide's single message. Aim for 8 to 12 slides. Don't design anything yet. Read the storyline out loud. If a slide's line doesn't push toward the one message, cut it. One slide, one message. If you can't say what a slide is for in one sentence, no tool will make it clear. 2. Pick your method There's no single best tool. There's the best tool for this deck. Claude: deck file or Slides Claude for PowerPoint Gamma Claude, then Gamma Best for A fast first draft from notes or a report Decks that must use your company template A designed look with little effort Strong words and a strong design Where you work A Claude chat Inside PowerPoint Gamma, in your browser Claude for words, Gamma for design What you get A .pptx file, or a Slides deck you can export Slides in your own master, fonts and colours A gamma you can present, share or export A Gamma deck with your exact wording Plan you need Claude Free works A paid Claude plan Gamma Free to start Both free plans to start A simple rule: Your company has a PowerPoint template? Use Claude for PowerPoint. You need it to look designed, and fast? Use Gamma. The words matter most? Plan in Claude, build in Gamma. You just need a quick .pptx? Ask Claude in a chat. Not sure which AI suits a job? Read this 3. Method 1a: Ask Claude for a deck file This is the quickest route, and it works on the Free plan. Claude can make PowerPoint (.pptx), Word, Excel and PDF files right in a conversation. You download the file, or save it straight to Google Drive. (Anthropic's help page.) Anthropic's built-in skills handle PowerPoint creation, and Claude uses them on its own when a request needs them. Step 1: Check file creation is on It's on by default for Free, Pro, Max and Ultra. Check once anyway. Open Settings, then Capabilities. Make sure Code execution and file creation is switched on. In the newer layout, the help page says it's called Create and edit files. Step 2: Give it your storyline and your content Paste the storyline from section 1, then your notes, or attach your report. Files can be up to 30MB each. Turn this storyline into a PowerPoint presentation (.pptx). Follow these rules. - One message per slide. Use the storyline line as the slide title, written as a full sentence. - No more than 30 words of body text per slide. - Where I give numbers, make a simple chart instead of a bullet list. - Use only the facts in my notes. If something is missing, leave a clear placeholder like [ADD FIGURE]. - Add speaker notes to each slide with what I should say. - Use a clean, plain design: white background, one accent colour. Storyline: [paste the storyline] Notes and numbers: [paste or attach] Step 3: Fix it in words Open the file. Then tell Claude what to change, one thing at a time. "Slide 4 has too much text. Split it into two slides." "Make the chart on slide 6 a bar chart." Each change gives you a new file to download. 4. Method 1b: Use Claude's Slides template Claude can also build a deck you work on right inside Claude. It's called an artifact: something Claude makes that you'd put in front of someone. It opens beside your conversation. Slides is one of the templates, and it's on every plan, Free included. (Anthropic's page on artifacts.) There are three ways to start one: Ask for a presentation in any chat. Select Output in the message box and choose the Slides template. Pick it in the Artifacts tab. Slides are built from your notes, your reports or the work already in your chat. So the storyline you wrote in section 1 can become the deck in the same conversation. Use the Slides template to turn the storyline above into a presentation. Keep my slide titles exactly as written. Keep body text short. Use the numbers I pasted earlier, and nothing else. What you can do with it: Edit slide by slide, by asking Claude or by typing on the slide yourself. Present it without leaving Claude. Export it: click Export to get PowerPoint or PDF, or send it straight to Google Slides as an editable file. Talking about…

title: Claude, from the first click.
subtitle: Never opened it? Everything you need for your first week, in plain words:
text: Everyone seems to be talking about Claude. You've never opened it. Or you opened it once, typed a question, and weren't sure what to do next. That's fine. This guide starts at zero and goes one step at a time. I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. So: plain words, real steps, and a picture wherever you need to find something on screen. By the end of this guide you'll have: Claude on your phone and your computer, on the right plan the few settings that matter, set once a simple way to ask that gets good answers a clear sense of what to trust and what to check one real task done, and eight ideas borrowed from professionals You need: a phone or a computer, an email address, and to be 18 or older. How to read it: sections 1 to 4 get you set up. Sections 5 to 9 teach you to use it well. Sections 10 to 13 are practice. 1. Meet Claude Claude is an AI assistant made by a company called Anthropic. Anthropic's help centre describes it as a large language model, trained to be helpful, honest and harmless, with a conversational tone. In plain words: you write to it the way you'd write to a person, and it writes back. It helps in two ways. It answers. Ask a quick question, get a quick answer, then ask a follow-up. It does the work. Describe the result you want, and Claude works through the steps: it searches the web, reads your files, runs code and hands back finished files. On paid plans, longer tasks keep running in the cloud if you close your laptop. Anthropic calls itself a public benefit corporation. Its stated mission is the responsible development of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. What it can make for you Most beginners undersell this. Claude doesn't only write replies. It makes things you can use: Files: Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF, to download or save to Google Drive. Spreadsheets come with working formulas. Artifacts: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard or a small interactive tool, opened beside the chat. Diagrams and charts: drawn in the chat on the web and desktop when you say "draw this as a diagram". Not sure where to start? Anthropic's own advice is to ask Claude what it can help with. Make it personal: I work as [your job]. A normal week for me includes [three or four tasks, for example writing reports, answering customer emails, planning events]. List ten specific ways you could help me this week. For each one, give me the exact first message I should send you. Start with the ones that would save me the most time. Use it in your first five minutes. You'll get ten jobs, each with a first message you can copy straight back in. Treat Claude like a capable new colleague. Give it a proper brief, and check its work before anything goes out under your name. 2. See how it differs from ChatGPT It's the first question most people ask. Here's a fair answer, built only from what each company publishes about its own product. Claude ChatGPT Free plan Yes, with limited usage every 5 hours and every week Yes, advertised as unlimited text chats with GPT-6, within abuse guardrails First paid plan Pro: $20 a month, or $17 a month paid yearly Plus: $20 a month Bigger plans Max at $100 and Ultra at $200 a month Pro 100, Pro 200 and Pro 500, at $100, $200 and $500 a month Ads None: Anthropic has committed to keeping Claude ad-free May appear on the Free and Go plans Making pictures No photos or illustrations; it makes diagrams, charts and visuals Image generation on every plan (limited on Free) Text it takes in at once Up to 1M tokens in chat on paid plans, with the newest models 27K to 128K tokens (GPT Instant) or 256K to 400K (GPT Reasoning), by plan A token is a small piece of text. For scale, Anthropic says 200K tokens is about 500 pages. What that means for you: You want pictures made? ChatGPT makes images. Claude doesn't. You work with long documents? Claude's paid plans take in more text at once. You'd rather not see ads? Anthropic has promised no ads and no sponsored links in Claude. (Its announcement, and OpenAI's page on ads.) Price? The first paid step costs the same: $20 a month. Coming from ChatGPT? Your old chats can't move over, but its memory of you can. Go to Settings → Your Claude and select Start import. Claude shows you a prompt to use in your old assistant. Paste the answer back and click Add to memory. Anthropic calls this experimental. Its guide is here. issue:right-ai-for-the-job 3. Get Claude and pick a plan Download and open it One account, three places: In a browser: go to claude.ai. On your computer: Claude Desktop, from claude.com/download. On your phone: search "Claude by Anthropic" in the App Store or the Play Store. Your conversations, projects, memory and preferences sync between them. Device Needs Mac macOS 13 (Ventura) or newer Windows Windows 10 or newer Linux (beta) Ubuntu 22.04 or newer, or Debian 12 or newer iPhone and iPad iOS or iPadOS 18.0 or newer Android Android 8.0 (Oreo) or newer You must be 18 or older and in a supported location. Nigeria, the United Kingdom and the United States are on Anthropic's list, with many others. Check yours here. A new account also needs a phone number from a supported location. Sign in There's no password. You get two ways in: Continue with Google: sign in with your Google account and click Next. Continue with email: type your email and click the button. Claude emails you a link titled "Secure link to log in to Claude.ai". Opened that email on another device? The link gives you a code instead. Type it on the device where you started. No email? Check your spam folder for a message from @mail.anthropic.com. Pick a plan Start on Free. It costs nothing and covers a lot. These are US prices: Anthropic shows local currency where it supports it. Prices exclude tax and can change. title: Cowork, from zero.
subtitle: You don't code? Good. Here's how to hand Claude real work, step by step:
text: You've used Claude to answer questions. Maybe to rewrite an email. Maybe to explain something. Then you hear that Claude can build a whole spreadsheet, or tidy a messy downloads folder, while you get on with something else. That's Cowork. And you don't need to write a single line of code to use it. I teach people to use AI at work. So this guide is plain words and real steps. Nothing technical. By the end of this guide you'll have: a clear picture of what Cowork is, and when to use it instead of chat the desktop app installed, with a safe folder set up for Claude one real task done, from a two-line request a better habit than long prompts: letting Claude interview you one plugin or connector added for your kind of work a short list of jobs to keep away from it You need: a paid Claude plan (Pro or above) and a Mac, Windows or Linux computer. 1. Know what Cowork is Cowork is Claude doing a whole job for you, not just answering one message. Anthropic describes it as bringing Claude Code's agentic abilities to knowledge work beyond coding. "Agentic" just means it can take steps on its own. Claude Code is the version for software engineers. Cowork uses the same approach for everyone else: research, analysis, documents. And it needs no terminal. Here's what happens when you give it a task: Claude reads your request and makes a plan. It breaks the work into smaller steps. It works through them in a private, temporary workspace on Anthropic's servers. It hands back finished files you can preview and download. You can watch what it's planning and doing the whole time. Step in when it matters. Or step away. That's the idea in one line: describe the outcome, step away, come back to finished work. What can "finished work" look like? Excel spreadsheets with working formulas. PowerPoint decks. Formatted documents. Organised folders. A research write-up. It reads most of the files you already use: Word, PDF, Excel, PowerPoint, CSV, plain text and common images. Chat is for questions. Cowork is for jobs. If you'd normally block out an hour for it, it's probably a Cowork task. 2. See how it differs from chat Here's the difference, side by side. Chat Cowork You give it a question or a prompt an outcome you want How it works one reply at a time plans, splits the job into steps, works through them Your files you upload them on desktop, it reads and writes files in folders you connect You get back an answer, sometimes a file finished files: spreadsheets, decks, documents, tidy folders While it works you wait for the reply you can close your laptop and check back later Plans every plan, including Free paid plans only Usage less more, because each step uses some One thing is changing. Anthropic is rolling out what it calls the "new Claude experience". In it, chat and Cowork merge into one conversation. There's no mode to pick. Claude decides what the job needs, and a quick question still gets a quick answer. How do you know if you have it? Look at the message box. If it no longer shows "Chat" and "Cowork" options, you have it. Everything in this guide still works. You just skip the step where you pick Cowork. New to Claude itself? Start here 3. Check your plan and install the app Cowork is on paid plans only: Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise. The Free plan gets chat, but not Cowork. The cheapest way in is Pro: $20 a month, or $17 a month if you pay for a year up front ($200). Prices exclude tax. (Claude's pricing page.) Where you can use it: Where Who gets Cowork Claude Desktop (Mac, Windows, Linux in beta) all paid plans Web and the Claude phone app Pro, Max, Ultra and Team (beta on Team); Enterprise if an owner turns it on Claude in Chrome side panel all paid plans Start with the desktop app. It's the only place Claude can reach the files on your computer. To install it: Go to claude.com/download. Pick your version: macOS, Windows, Windows (arm 64) or the Microsoft Store. Linux links to setup docs instead. Install it and sign in with your Claude account. Check your computer first. You need macOS 13 (Ventura) or later, or Windows 10 or later. On Linux, Cowork also needs about 25 GB of free disk space and at least 8 GB of memory. (Install Claude Desktop.) 4. Give Claude a folder of its own On desktop, Claude can read and write your files directly. No uploading, no downloading. But only in folders you connect. Anthropic's own advice: make a dedicated working folder for Claude, rather than giving it broad access. And keep backups of anything important. So do this before your first task: Make a new folder. Call it something like "Claude Work". Copy in the files for one real job. Copies, not originals. When Claude asks which folder to use, point it here. There's a safety net too. Claude has to ask your permission, with an "Allow" prompt, before it permanently deletes any file. Your files stay on your computer. When a task needs one, Claude fetches a copy of just that file, and those copies are deleted when you delete the session. Set Cowork up properly, step by step 5. Run your first task Here's how to start, in the desktop app: In the message box, select Cowork. Describe the task. Read Claude's plan, then let it run. Before you send it, choose how much Claude checks with you. There's a setting for this in the message box, with three options: Option What Claude does Use it when Manually approve pauses and asks you to Allow or Deny actions your first tasks, and anything sensitive Automatically approve keeps going, and screens each action for safety, blocking unsafe ones everyday work you've done before Skip all approvals nothing checks its actions almost never: only when you fully trust every file, app and connector involved "Automatically approve" is rolling out as the default on Pro, Max, Ultra and Team. For your very first task, pick Manually approve. You'll see every step Claude wants to take. It's the fastest way to learn what it does. Once the task is running, you don't have to sit and watch. Sessions…

title: Give every job a home.
subtitle: Cowork projects, from your first one to three you'll use every week:
text: You use Cowork for real work now. A report here. Some research there. A proposal on Friday. And every time, you explain the same things again. Who the client is. Which folder to use. How you like the numbers laid out. Projects fix that. A project is one home for one kind of work. It keeps the files, the rules and what Claude has learned, so the next task starts where the last one stopped. I teach people to use AI at work. This guide gives you the set-up, the prompts and the limits, in plain words. By the end of this guide you'll have: a clear picture of what a Cowork project holds your first project, created the right way three ready workflows, with prompts, for reporting, research and sales proposals a simple rule for when a classic chat project is still the better choice a 15-minute set-up you can do today You need: a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Ultra, Team or Enterprise), because Cowork isn't on Free the latest version of Claude Desktop, from claude.com/download one piece of work you repeat every week or month New to Cowork? Start with Cowork, from zero, then come back. 1. What goes inside a project Cowork takes on multi-step work for you. You describe the result, step away, and come back to finished work: a formatted document, organised files, a research summary. A project wraps that work in a workspace. Anthropic's help centre puts it simply: a project groups related tasks into a dedicated workspace with its own files, context, instructions and memory. Each project has four parts: Part What it does Instructions Tone, formatting or rules that guide every task in the project Context A local folder, a linked chat project, or a URL for Claude to reference Memory What Claude learns from tasks here, applied to future tasks here Scheduled tasks Recurring tasks that belong to this project only New projects you create in Cowork are saved to your Claude account. So you can pick them up from your other devices. The help centre also says projects work the same way in Cowork and in Claude. One project per kind of work. Weekly reporting gets one. Each big client gets one. Mixing them is how Claude ends up using the wrong numbers. 2. Pick your way in There are three ways to create a project. Pick by where your material already lives. If... Choose What happens The work is new Start from scratch You set up a new folder with instructions and files You already have a classic chat project for it Import from project Its files and instructions move into a new Cowork project The files already sit in a folder on your computer Use an existing folder That folder becomes the project's context A few details worth knowing before you click: Import from project shows a "Search projects in Chat..." field. Click into it to see recent projects, or search all of them. You can import one chat project at a time. Bulk upload isn't supported. With both import and an existing folder, you name the new project and choose where to save it on your computer. Use an existing folder only if that folder holds just this one job. Anthropic advises giving Claude a dedicated working folder instead of broad access. If your folder is a messy mix, start from scratch and copy in what belongs. 3. Click through the set-up Here's the click path, in words first. In Claude Desktop, find Projects in the left navigation panel. Click the + button. Choose Start from scratch, Import from project or Use an existing folder. Give the project a clear name, such as "Weekly sales report". Add instructions and attach any files you want it to start with. Click Create. How to check it worked: the new project appears under Projects, and opening it shows its own page with Instructions, Context, Memory and Scheduled tasks. If your message box no longer shows "Chat" and "Cowork" options, you have the new Claude experience. The help centre says some steps may look a little different there. Not set up Cowork yet? Do that first 4. Write the instructions and add context An empty project is just a folder with a name. The instructions are what make it useful. Write them like a note to a new colleague who will do this job every week. What's the job, who reads the result, what does good look like? You don't have to write them alone. Let Claude interview you. I'm setting up a Cowork project for [the job, e.g. our monthly marketing report]. Interview me, one question at a time, until you understand: - who reads the result and what they decide with it - the files and sources I use - the format, length and tone I want - the mistakes I don't want repeated Then write short project instructions, readable in one minute, that I can paste into this project's Instructions. Then add Context. You have three options: a local folder with the files this job uses a linked chat project, if you keep reference material there a URL, such as a public page Claude should always check These instructions sit on top of your global instructions. Global ones apply to every Cowork session: your role, your usual tone. Set them at Settings → Cowork → Edit next to Global instructions. In the new Claude experience, they're part of Instructions for Claude in Settings → Your Claude. So keep the global ones about you, and the project ones about the job. When you select a local folder on desktop, Claude can also keep folder instructions and update them itself during a session. Read them now and then, so you know what it's following. guide:brief-claude-like-a-colleague 5. Decide what it remembers Memory is on for Cowork projects. Claude remembers context from tasks you run in a project and applies it to later tasks in the same project. What it learns in one project doesn't carry over to other projects. But here's the part most people miss: a project also shares memory with your chats outside projects. That's handy for a personal workflow. It's less handy for client work. To keep a project fully separate: Open the project's page. Go to Memory. Turn off Use account memory. A simple rule: client, HR or…

title: Infographics that stay sharp.
subtitle: Clear, editable one-page visuals with AI, and a template your team can reuse:
text: You need a one-page visual for a report, a post or a slide. You ask an AI image tool for it. It looks great at first glance. Then you spot a wrong word, or a number you need to change. And there's no way to fix one word in a picture. You make the whole thing again. There's a better way for most infographics: build them as code. An infographic built in HTML and SVG is a web page. Every word is real text. Every colour is a setting. You fix it by asking for the change in plain words. I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. This is the method I'd show a team that makes visuals every week. By the end of this guide you'll have: a clear rule for when to use Claude and when to use an image generator your first infographic, built as code, with text you can edit a way to add an illustration without losing sharp text a project or a skill so your team gets the same look every time You need: a Claude account (artifacts are on every plan, Free included) the words and numbers your infographic should show for illustrations only: an account with an image generator, such as ChatGPT or Gemini 1. Pick the right tool for each part Most infographics are words, numbers and simple shapes. Some also need a picture: a person, a scene, an object. Those are two different jobs, and they suit two different tools. Anthropic is clear about what Claude does here. It doesn't generate photos or illustrations the way image tools do. It builds diagrams, charts and interactive visuals with HTML and SVG. (Anthropic's page.) Image generators do the opposite job well. ChatGPT lists image generation on every plan, limited on Free. In the Gemini app, the Nano Banana 2 image model is free. Part of the infographic Best tool Why Headings, labels, numbers Claude, as code Real text: change one word without redrawing anything Charts, timelines, flows Claude, as code Shapes follow your numbers, and you can check them Brand colours and fonts Claude, as code One setting changes every block Photos, scenes, characters An image generator Claude doesn't make photos or illustrations A mix of both Picture first, then Claude The picture sits inside a layout of live text A simple rule: if you'd ever need to edit it, build it as code. Words and numbers belong in code. Pictures belong in an image generator. Keep them apart and your infographic stays easy to fix. 2. Switch on file creation Claude's artifacts need one setting turned on. Here's where it is: Open Settings. Go to Capabilities. Switch on Code execution and file creation. Anthropic's help page says the updated layout calls this setting Create and edit files. If you see that name, it's the same switch. How to check it worked: in a new chat, ask Claude to "draw this as a diagram" with three short lines of text. You should see a visual appear in the conversation. One more thing to know: custom visuals in chat work on the web and the desktop app. They don't show in the iOS or Android apps. Build your infographics on a computer. New to Claude? Start here 3. Write the words before the design This is the step most people skip. They ask for "an infographic about our results", and the AI fills the gaps with filler. An infographic is only as good as its content. So write the content first, as plain text. Keep it tight: One message. What should the reader remember after five seconds? One reader. Who is it for, and where will they see it? Five to seven blocks. Each one is a heading plus one or two lines. Every number with its source. If you can't say where it came from, leave it out. If your notes are messy, let Claude help you shape them before any design. Here are my notes for a one-page infographic: [paste your notes, figures and sources] It's for [who will see it], who will see it on [LinkedIn / a slide / a printed report]. Before any design, write the content only: 1. A title of no more than eight words. 2. A one-line subtitle. 3. Five to seven blocks, each with a heading of three to five words and one or two short lines. 4. A source line for every number. Use only the facts in my notes. If something is missing or unclear, ask me instead of guessing. Read what comes back slowly. Cut anything you wouldn't say out loud to the reader. Fewer blocks almost always look better. If you have ten points, you have two infographics. 4. Ask Claude to build it as code Now ask for the design, and say clearly that you want code. You have two ways to do it. A quick visual in the chat You don't need to turn anything on. Ask with words like "draw this as a diagram" or "chart this data", and Claude draws the visual inline. These visuals are built with HTML and are temporary by default. To keep one, use one of the options Anthropic lists: Copy as image Download, as an .svg or .html file Save as artifact (Anthropic's page on custom visuals.) An artifact you can edit and share An artifact is anything Claude makes that you'd put in front of someone. It opens beside the conversation, and you can edit and share it. Artifacts come with templates. Design is on every plan, and it's the natural home for an infographic. Here's a prompt that gets a clean first version: Build this as a one-page infographic in HTML and SVG. Content (use it exactly, don't add facts): [paste the title, subtitle, blocks and sources from step 3] Design: - Size: [1080 x 1350 for LinkedIn / 1920 x 1080 for a slide / A4 portrait for print] - Colours: [your two or three brand colours, as hex codes, or "one dark colour and one accent"] - Font: [your font, or "a clean sans-serif"] - Layout: a clear title at the top, the blocks in a grid, sources in small text at the bottom - Leave plenty of space around each block Rules: - Keep every word as real, editable text. No text inside images. - Draw charts and icons in SVG, not as pictures. - Make sure nothing overlaps or gets cut off at the edges. title: Set up Cowork once.
subtitle: Already tried Cowork? Set it up properly in one sitting, and stop babysitting it:
text: You've tried Cowork a few times. It did something useful. Then it asked you a lot of questions, saved files in odd places, and ate a chunk of your usage. Cowork works fine. It just hasn't been set up yet. I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. This guide is the set-up I'd want every professional to do once. It takes about 20 minutes. You won't have to do it again. By the end of this guide you'll have: one working folder Claude can use, laid out so you always know where things are global instructions, written from a template, that every session reads an approval mode that fits the work you do a way of handing over whole tasks, so you review instead of steering every step a few habits that make your usage allowance last one real task done, in your first 20 minutes You need: a paid Claude plan: Pro, Max, Ultra, Team or Enterprise (Cowork isn't on Free) Claude Desktop on your computer, if you want Claude to work with your own files one small, real job you'd happily hand to a capable colleague New to Cowork? Start with Cowork, from zero and come back here. Why the set-up matters Cowork isn't a chat that answers one prompt at a time. Anthropic describes it as bringing Claude Code's agentic abilities to knowledge work beyond coding. It takes on multi-step tasks. The way it's meant to work is simple: you describe an outcome, step away, and come back to finished work. When a task starts, Claude makes a plan, breaks the work into smaller tasks, runs them in an isolated environment on Anthropic's servers, may run some of them in parallel, and hands you the results. It can make Excel spreadsheets with working formulas, PowerPoint presentations and formatted documents. So the quality of what you get depends on three things you control: what Claude can reach (your folder) what Claude knows about you (your instructions) how you hand the work over (whole tasks, clear finish line) Get those right once, and every task after that starts from a better place. The slow part of Cowork is rarely Claude. It's the person checking every step. The set-up below moves you from steering to reviewing. 1. Check what you have First, find out which version of Claude you're on. It changes a few menu names in this guide. Open Claude and look at the message box. You see 'Chat' and 'Cowork' options. Select Cowork, describe the task, read Claude's approach and let it run. You don't see them. You have the new Claude experience. Chat and Cowork are one conversation, with no mode to pick. Just describe the task. Both are fine. Where a menu differs, I'll give you both paths. Install Claude Desktop Cowork runs in the cloud. Your sessions and files are saved to your Claude account, so work carries on if you close your laptop. But Claude can only read and write the files on your computer through Claude Desktop. Download it from claude.com/download. Keep two rules in mind: a task that uses your local files needs the desktop app open on that computer a task that doesn't touch your files keeps running when the app is closed or the computer is asleep Check it worked: open Claude Desktop, sign in, and start a new conversation. If you see the 'Cowork' option or an empty message box ready for a task, you're set. guide:cowork-from-zero 2. Make one working folder This is the step most people skip. It's also the one that saves the most time. Anthropic's own advice is to create a dedicated working folder for Claude instead of giving it broad access to your computer. And to keep backups of important files. Claude can only read and write in folders you've connected. So one tidy folder means Claude always knows where to look, and you always know where to find the result. A layout that works Make one folder called Claude work (or any name you like). Inside it, make four folders: Folder What goes in Who writes in it Inbox Files you want Claude to work on this week You Reference Things Claude should read but never change: templates, style notes, past examples You Output Everything Claude makes Claude Archive Finished work you want to keep You Then connect only the Claude work folder. Why this layout: Inbox and Output are separate, so Claude never overwrites the files you gave it Reference holds your examples, so you can say "match the format in Reference" instead of explaining it again Archive keeps Output short, so Claude isn't reading old work by mistake What Claude can and can't do with it Your folders stay on your computer. When a cloud task needs a file, Claude fetches a copy of just that file. Those copies are deleted when you delete the session. Claude must ask you with an Allow prompt before it permanently deletes any file. Claude reads single files up to 50 MB. In the new Claude experience, Settings shows where Cowork saved its work as Storage folder, and the folders you gave it as Trusted folders. Let Claude build it for you Connect an empty folder, then paste this. In the folder I've connected, create four folders: Inbox, Reference, Output and Archive. Then add a short file called README.md in the main folder that explains, in plain words: - Inbox: files I want you to work on - Reference: files you read but never change - Output: where you save everything you make - Archive: finished work I keep From now on, save everything you make in Output, and never change or delete anything in Reference. Show me the folder list when you're done. Check it worked: open the folder on your computer. You should see the four folders and the README file. If you rename or move a connected folder, Claude may lose it. On a recent Claude Desktop on macOS 14 or later, Claude can find it and ask you to Keep connected. On Windows, Linux or older macOS, you must connect it again. (Anthropic's note on renamed folders.) 3. Tell Claude how you work Global instructions are standing instructions that apply to every Cowork session. Anthropic suggests three things to put in them: your tone, your output format, and…

title: Stop running out of Claude.
subtitle: Hit the limit mid-task? How usage is counted, and twelve habits that make it last:
text: You're halfway through a real piece of work. Then Claude tells you you've reached your limit. The report isn't finished. The deadline hasn't moved. Most people blame the plan. Often the cause is the way they're using Claude. I teach people to use AI at work, and my mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone. So this guide sticks to what Anthropic's own help pages say, in plain words. By the end of this guide you'll know: how your usage is actually counted where to see how much you have left what uses it up fastest twelve habits that use less, each one small what to do when you hit the limit anyway You need: a Claude account, on any plan, and five minutes to look at your own settings. 1. Know the two kinds of limit Claude has two different limits. Mixing them up is where most confusion starts. Usage limits are your budget over time. Anthropic's help centre calls it a "conversation budget": how much you can use Claude across all your chats before you wait for a reset. Length limits are about one single chat. Each chat can only hold so much text at once. That space is called the context window. They have different fixes. So it helps to know which one you've hit. Usage limit Length limit What it measures How much you use Claude over time, across all chats How much fits in one chat When it ends When the five-hour session or the weekly limit resets It doesn't: you move to a new chat Does upgrading help? Yes: the new plan's limits apply right away No Anthropic's fix Wait for the reset, or use less Start a new conversation, or use projects A usage limit is about time. A length limit is about one chat. Upgrading only helps with the first. 2. See how usage is counted Here's how it works on most accounts, from Anthropic's own pages. The five-hour session. Your session starts with your first message. It resets in full five hours later. The weekly limit. Paid plans also have a weekly limit. It resets at a fixed day and time assigned to your account, whenever you start using Claude. One pool. Claude on the web, on the desktop app, on your phone and in Claude Code all draw from the same allowance. Voice mode counts too. No fixed number of messages. There's no message count to keep track of. On the Free plan, the number of messages you get varies with demand. Weekly limits cover every model. Some plans also have a separate weekly limit for Fable models. One more thing to know. Anthropic says it may adjust limits to manage capacity, so they can change. Where to check Open Settings, then Usage. Under Current session, a bar shows how much of your five-hour allowance is left. The same page shows when your next weekly reset is. Look at this page before a big job, not after. If the session bar is nearly full, start the big job after the reset. 3. Know what uses it fastest Every message doesn't cost the same. Anthropic lists the things that use your limit faster: long messages big attachments long conversations tools, such as Research and web search the model you choose a higher effort level artifacts (the documents, slides and other things Claude makes beside the chat) multi-step tasks Two of these surprise people. Long chats cost more as they grow. Anthropic's Claude Code guide explains why: every turn sends the whole conversation so far back to Claude, plus your new message. The conversation is the part that grows fastest. So the later messages in a long chat cost more than the early ones. Links can be heavy. Web search and web fetch count toward your limits. A link to a long article pulls the entire article into the chat. Anthropic's example: summarising a 10,000-word article uses substantially more than a regular web search. And one thing works in your favour. Files in a project are cached, so they count less against your limits when you reuse them. That cache expires after a while without use. New to Claude? Start here 4. Ask less, ask better The first four habits are about your messages. Anthropic's own usage tips come down to this: fewer, fuller messages. Tip 1. Put related questions in one message Five short messages cost more than one complete one, because each new message carries the chat so far with it. So collect your questions first. Then send them together. I'm preparing a 10-minute update for my team on our new expense policy. Please: 1. Summarise the attached policy in five bullet points. 2. List the three changes most likely to confuse people. 3. Suggest one question I should be ready to answer. Tip 2. Give the background up front When Claude has to guess, you end up correcting it. Every correction is another message. Say who it's for, what it's for and what good looks like, in the first message. Anthropic's prompting guide has a simple test: would a colleague with no context understand your request? If they'd be confused, Claude will be too. Tip 3. Batch similar jobs Got six emails to draft, or ten product descriptions to tidy? Ask for all of them in one message, not one per message. Below are six customer emails, separated by lines of dashes. For each one, write a short, polite reply in plain English. Keep each reply under 80 words. Number the replies to match the emails. Tip 4. Read it once before you send Ten seconds of checking saves a follow-up. Is the file attached? Did you say how long the answer should be? Did you say the format: table, bullets, an email? Anthropic's advice is to be specific about the format and constraints, and to ask for more than the minimum if you want it. 5. Keep your chats lean The next four habits stop a chat from growing heavier than it needs to be. Tip 5. New task, new chat When you move to a different job, open a new chat. The old chat's history doesn't help the new task. It just gets carried along and counted. Tip 6. Hand over before a chat gets too long When a long chat gets close to its length limit, Claude automatically summarises the earlier messages so it can keep going. That uses more of your usage limit.
